Ce verset rapporte que, au Jour de la Résurrection, Dieu rappelle à Jésus, fils de Marie, les bienfaits qu'il lui a accordés ainsi qu'à sa mère : il l'a soutenu par l'Esprit saint, lui a permis de parler aux gens dans le berceau et à l'âge mûr, lui a enseigné l'Écriture, la sagesse, la Torah et l'Évangile, et l'a fait façonner dans l'argile une forme d'oiseau qui, par son souffle et avec la permission de Dieu, devenait un oiseau vivant ; il guérissait l'aveugle-né et le lépreux et ressuscitait les morts avec la permission divine, et il a empêché les fils d'Israël de s'en prendre à lui lorsqu'il leur apporta les preuves, alors que les incrédules parmi eux dirent : ceci n'est que magie manifeste. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que tous ces prodiges se sont accomplis par la permission de Dieu et non par la puissance propre de Jésus, d'où la répétition de « par Ma permission ». Ils s'accordent aussi sur le sens de ce passage : un rappel de grâce adressé à Jésus, à la fois reproche aux juifs qui l'ont rejeté et aux chrétiens qui l'ont exalté. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi expliquent « je t'ai fortifié » par « je t'ai soutenu », et voient en l'Esprit saint Gabriel. Al-Razi et al-Baydawi proposent aussi que l'Esprit saint désigne une âme pure ou la parole qui vivifie la religion. Pour le mot « kahl », certains l'entendent comme l'âge compris entre trente et cinquante ans, et en tirent l'idée d'une future descente de Jésus. Sur la lecture, Hamza et al-Kisa'i lisent « sâhir », ce qui vise Jésus lui-même, tandis que la majorité lit « siḥr », qui vise ce qu'il apporta. Al-Razi remarque que la mention des incrédules dans ce contexte de bienfaits s'explique par l'envie qui accompagne toute grâce, et qu'elle en souligne ainsi la grandeur. Les questions de l'au-delà, comme la manière exacte de la résurrection, ne sont pas tranchées par les commentateurs et restent dans le domaine du mystère.

Dieu rappelle à Jésus un autre de ses bienfaits : il a inspiré aux apôtres, les disciples sincères (al-Hawariyyun), de croire en lui et en son messager. Ils ont répondu : « Nous croyons, et sois témoin que nous sommes soumis à Dieu. » Sur le sens du mot « inspiration » (wahy), les commentateurs divergent. Al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir et d'autres y voient une inspiration intérieure, un jet dans les cœurs, comme le disent al-Suddi et al-Hasan. Abu 'Ubayda y voit un ordre transmis par les messagers ; d'autres associent les deux sens, l'ordre passant par Jésus et l'inspiration touchant les cœurs. Al-Baydawi et Ibn 'Atiyya tiennent « an » pour explicative. Quant au « sois témoin » adressé à Dieu chez al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya et Ibn al-Jawzi, certains le lisent comme une adresse à Jésus.

Al-Razi explique que ce passage vise à reprendre les chrétiens : chacun de ces bienfaits montre que Jésus est un serviteur et non un dieu. Les commentateurs s'accordent à dire que les apôtres étaient sincèrement croyants. Ils diffèrent sur le sens du mot « hawariyyun » : al-Hasan les dit foulons, Mujahid pêcheurs, 'Ikrima des élus, et Qatada des ministres. Al-Razi remarque que la foi est mentionnée avant la soumission parce que la foi relève du cœur et la soumission de l'extérieur. Ibn Sa'di souligne la même idée en unissant l'islam extérieur et la foi intérieure.

La mention des apôtres prépare le récit de la table descendue du ciel. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Zamakhshari rapportent que ceux-ci demandèrent ce miracle, certains commentateurs disant que cette demande précéda leur vue des signes, d'autres qu'elle suivit leur foi.

Les commentateurs expliquent que les disciples (al-hawariyyun) demandèrent à Jésus si son Seigneur pouvait faire descendre sur eux une table servie du ciel. Le sens général de la demande est que les disciples souhaitaient qu'il prie son Seigneur d'accorder cette faveur, et Jésus leur répondit en leur ordonnant de craindre Dieu s'ils étaient croyants. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Baghawi s'accordent pour dire que les disciples ne doutaient pas de la puissance divine : ils voulaient être rassurés ou obtenir une réponse à leur prière, car le verbe « pouvoir » peut signifier « obéir » ou « exaucer ». Al-Zamakhshari, en revanche, prend l'expression au pied de la lettre et estime que les disciples n'étaient pas sincèrement croyants ; Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi et d'autres le contredisent et soutiennent qu'ils étaient croyants et que leurs propos étaient simplement mal formulés. La lecture de al-Kisa'i, attribuée à 'Ali, 'A'isha et Ibn 'Abbas, qui lit « tastati'u rabbaka » (peux-tu demander à ton Seigneur), est souvent présentée comme écartant la difficulté.

Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens du mot « mā'ida » : une table garnie de nourriture, dont l'étymologie est discutée entre le fait de donner (mādā) et celui de bouger (māda). Sur la nature de la table, les avis divergent : Ibn 'Abbas parle d'un poisson et de pains, d'autres d'une nourriture sans viande, et al-Hasan et Mujahid affirment que la table n'est jamais descendue. Ibn Kathir et al-Tabari retiennent au contraire la descente, en s'appuyant sur les paroles divines « je la ferai descendre sur vous » et sur des récits rapportés d'après 'Ammar ibn Yasir ; ils mentionnent aussi l'avertissement contre la trahison et la thésaurisation.

Enfin, la réponse « craignez Dieu » est interprétée soit comme une mise en garde contre la demande de miracles après la foi, soit comme un rappel à ne pas douter de la puissance divine, soit encore comme une invitation à ne pas réclamer ce qu'aucune nation n'a demandé avant eux.

Ce verset rapporte la demande des apôtres à Jésus, qui souhaitaient qu'il invoque Dieu pour faire descendre une table du ciel. Les commentateurs expliquent que leur but était de manger, de voir leur cœur apaisé, de savoir avec certitude que Jésus disait vrai et d'en être témoins auprès de ceux qui n'étaient pas présents. Ibn 'Abbas et d'autres attribuent ce désir à une faim pressante, tandis qu'al-Mawardi et Ibn al-Jawzi rapportent aussi l'avis selon lequel ils voulaient surtout la bénédiction de ce repas. Al-Mawardi s'appuie sur le fait que, s'ils avaient eu faim, on ne les aurait pas blâmés pour cette demande. Concernant la formule « هل يستطيع ربك », certains, dont Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi et Ibn al-Anbari, affirment qu'il ne s'agissait pas d'un doute sur la puissance divine mais d'une façon de demander si Dieu accepterait, tandis qu'az-Zamakhshari y voit l'expression d'un doute réel de leur part. La lecture attribuée à al-Kisa'i et à 'Aisha, « هل تستطيع ربك », signifierait « peux-tu demander à ton Seigneur ». Quant au mot « نعلم », les avis divergent : certains y voient une connaissance nouvelle acquise par ce signe, d'autres une augmentation de certitude. Dans l'ensemble, les commentateurs s'accordent sur le sens général du passage et diffèrent surtout sur l'interprétation des termes.

Ce verset rapporte la prière de Jésus, fils de Marie, lorsque les disciples lui demandèrent une table descendue du ciel. Il invoqua son Seigneur pour qu'elle descende, afin qu'en son jour, les premiers comme les derniers d'entre eux en fassent une fête, et qu'elle soit un signe venant de Dieu ; il demanda aussi à être pourvu, car Dieu est le meilleur des pourvoyeurs. Les commentateurs s'accordent à voir dans cette prière la réponse à la demande des disciples. Le sens de « fête » (ʿīd) est lui-même discuté : al-Sudi, Qatada et Sufyan y voient un jour que l'on honore et où l'on prie, Ibn ʿAbbas explique que tous, premiers et derniers, mangeront de la table, al-Zamakhshari et Ibn ʿAtiyya comprennent une joie qui revient, al-Khalil un jour de rassemblement. Ibn Kathir et al-Baghawi rapportent que le dimanche est le jour de la descente, ce qui explique que les chrétiens en aient fait une fête.

Les savants divergent sur la descente même de la table. Mujahid et al-Hasan affirment qu'elle ne descendit pas, car les disciples, effrayés par la menace de châtiment pour quiconque renierait après la descente, renoncèrent à leur demande. La majorité, dont al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et al-Razi, soutient qu'elle descendit, car Dieu dit « je la ferai descendre sur vous », et Sa promesse ne manque pas. Quant à sa nature, les récits varient : pain et poisson, un poisson au goût de tout mets, des fruits du paradis, ou encore le fait que certains volèrent et qu'ils furent transformés en singes et en porcs. Plusieurs de ces récits sont jugés faibles par Ibn Kathir et d'autres commentateurs.

Dieu rapporte à Jésus, fils de Marie, qu'il fera descendre la table servie sur les Apôtres, et que quiconque d'entre eux mécroira après cela subira un châtiment tel qu'il n'en infligera jamais de semblable à aucun des mondes. Les commentateurs s'accordent sur le fait que la menace vise celui qui nie après avoir vu le signe, car sa faute est plus grave. Ils divergent en revanche sur la réalité de la descente. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi et al-Qurtubi tiennent qu'elle a bien eu lieu, car Dieu l'annonce sous la forme d'une promesse certaine, et que le serment de la menace ne la contredit pas. Al-Hasan et Mujahid soutiennent au contraire qu'elle n'est jamais descendue, les Apôtres ayant renoncé dès qu'ils ont entendu la condition ; Mujahid y voit même une parabole donnée aux hommes pour les détourner de réclamer des signes. Quant à la nature de la table, les récits sont nombreux et divergents : Ibn 'Abbas et Atta y placent du pain et du poisson, 'Ammar ibn Yasir des pains et de la viande ou des fruits du Paradis, Sa'id ibn Jubayr tout aliment sauf la viande. Ibn Kathir et Abu Hayyan jugent la plupart de ces récits fragiles et n'en retiennent que ce qui est attesté. Plusieurs commentateurs, dont al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi, expliquent que la menace peut se réaliser dans ce monde par la métamorphose en singes et en porcs, ou dans l'au-delà, et que « les mondes » désignent les hommes de leur époque ou l'ensemble des créatures. Ibn 'Ashur voit surtout dans ce passage une leçon sur la foi des Apôtres et sur la valeur de la promesse divine, en laissant de côté les détails de la table.

Ce verset rapporte qu'Allah interroge Jésus, fils de Marie, sur la croyance des chrétiens selon laquelle il serait lui et sa mère deux divinités en dehors d'Allah. Jésus répond par la glorification de Dieu et par son désaveu, en remettant la science à Allah. Les commentateurs divergent sur le moment de ce dialogue. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj et la majorité des exégètes, dont Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi et Ibn al-Jawzi, estiment qu'il aura lieu le Jour de la Résurrection, pour confondre les chrétiens devant toutes les créatures, en s'appuyant sur le contexte et sur la suite du verset : « C'est un jour où la véracité profite aux véridiques. » Al-Sudda et al-Tabari pensent qu'il a eu lieu au moment où Allah éleva Jésus vers Lui, al-Tabari se fondant sur la particule « idh », qui marque le passé, tandis qu'Ibn Kathir juge que la condition n'implique pas la réalisation de l'acte. Tous s'accordent à dire que l'interrogation vise la réprimande et non l'information, et que Jésus n'a pas tenu ces propos. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi et al-Baydawi expliquent qu'on parle de deux divinités même si les chrétiens n'ont pas divinisé Marie, car ils ont fait de l'enfant un dieu, ce qui implique la même chose pour sa mère. Al-Razi et al-Alusi notent que le mot « dun » indique soit la différence soit l'association. Quant au mot « nafs », Ibn 'Abbas et la plupart y voient le secret ou l'inconnu, al-Zajjaj la réalité intime, al-Zamakhshari et al-Baydawi une figure de style par correspondance, tandis qu'al-Alusi et al-Shawkani refusent de l'appliquer à l'essence divine sans cette correspondance. Ces lectures convergent pour affirmer la servitude de Jésus et l'étendue du savoir divin.

Ce verset rapporte la réponse de Jésus, que Dieu interroge sur la prétention de ses adorateurs qui le tenaient, lui et sa mère, pour deux divinités en dehors d'Allah. Jésus se défend en affirmant qu'il n'a dit que ce que Dieu lui avait ordonné : adorer Allah, son Seigneur et le leur. Les commentateurs divergent sur le moment de ce dialogue : al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir et la majorité des exégètes, comme Qatada et Ibn Abbas, le placent le Jour de la Résurrection devant toute l'humanité, tandis que al-Suddi, et un avis rapporté par al-Tabari, le situent au moment où Dieu éleva Jésus vers le ciel.

Le mot tawaffi suscite lui aussi des interprétations. La plupart des commentateurs, dont al-Razi, Ibn Kathir et al-Baydawi, y voient l'élévation de Jésus au ciel. Al-Hasan rappelle que le terme désigne aussi la mort et le sommeil. Al-Jubba'i, lui, comprend qu'il s'agit d'une mort véritable, opinion qu'Ibn Kathir n'accepte pas.

Les exégètes s'accordent sur le sens de raqib, le gardien qui veille sur les actes des gens, et sur le fait que Dieu est témoin de toute chose. Ils divergent sur la portée de la demande de pardon : certains expliquent qu'elle vise un pardon par repentir avant la mort, d'autres, comme al-Razi et Ibn Juzayy, y voient une remise totale de l'affaire à la volonté divine. Al-Zamakhshari souligne que le nom al-'Aziz al-Hakim convient mieux au contexte de soumission que al-Ghafur al-Rahim.

Sur le plan linguistique, les commentateurs débattent de la fonction de la particule 'an dans « an u'budu Allah », qui peut être explicative, ou un complément du pronom, et Al-Zamakhshari et Abu Hayyan discutent longuement de ces analyses.

Ce verset rapporte la parole que Dieu adresse à Jésus le jour de la Résurrection, puis la réponse de Jésus, qui se dégage de toute divinisation de lui-même et de sa mère et remet le sort des hommes entre les mains de Dieu. Le sens général, tel que le donnent les exégètes : si Dieu châtie ceux qui sont morts dans l'incroyance, ils sont Ses serviteurs et nul ne peut Lui demander de comptes ; s'il pardonne à ceux qui se repentent et croient, c'est qu'Il est le Puissant, que rien ne contrarie, et le Sage, qui n'agit que avec sagesse. La plupart s'accordent à voir dans ces mots une remise du jugement à Dieu plutôt qu'une demande de pardon explicite, ce qui explique que Jésus ne dise pas « le Pardonneur, le Miséricordieux ». Al-Tabari et Ibn Kathir situent la scène au Jour dernier, al-Tabari ajoutant qu'elle pourrait avoir eu lieu au moment de l'élévation de Jésus, en s'appuyant sur le temps du verbe ; Ibn Kathir retient la première lecture. Ibn 'Ashur et al-Tabari voient dans la question adressée aux chrétiens un moyen de les confondre. Al-Razi affirme que le pardon de l'associationnisme est possible en soi selon la doctrine sunnite et selon la majorité des mu'tazilites basrites, et que le conditionnel de la phrase n'implique pas qu'il arrive. Al-Qurtubi et Ibn Kathir rapportent le hadith d'Abu Dharr, où le Prophète ﷺ récita ce verset toute la nuit en priant pour sa communauté. Ibn al-Qayyim y voit une politesse envers Dieu, car le pardon procède de la pleine puissance et de la pleine science. Ibn 'Uthaymin précise que la servitude visée est celle de la création. La variante « le Pardonneur, le Miséricordieux », attestée dans certains codex, n'est pas retenue dans le texte coranique ; les commentateurs y voient une cohérence préservée par les attributs de puissance et de sagesse.

Les commentateurs expliquent que Dieu déclare que ce jour, le Jour de la Résurrection, est celui où la véracité des véridiques leur sera profitable : il leur accorde des jardins sous lesquels coulent les rivières, où ils demeureront éternellement, Dieu étant satisfait d'eux et eux de Lui, ce qui constitue la grande réussite. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir et la plupart des autres s'accordent à dire que ce jour est celui de la Résurrection et que la véracité visée est celle de la vie d'ici-bas, comme tenir ses engagements, croire aux messagers et les confirmer, et être sincère dans ses actes. Al-Mawardi explique que cette véracité peut porter sur les engagements, sur la confirmation des prophètes, sur le témoignage rendu aux prophètes quant à la transmission du message, ou sur l'aveu de ses propres actes. Quant à la lecture, Nafi' est le seul à lire « yawma » à l'accusatif. Al-Tabari et al-Zajjaj l'expliquent comme un complément de temps. Les Kufiens admettent que le mot soit indéclinable à cause de sa construction avec un verbe, mais les Basriens le refusent, et al-Tabari retient la lecture au nominatif, suivie par la majorité des lecteurs. Ibn 'Atiyya et al-Zamakhshari estiment que ces paroles concernent surtout Jésus, tandis que la plupart des exégètes y voient une règle générale pour tout véridique. Al-Razi affirme que le Paradis, comparé à l'agrément divin, est presque néant, et il met donc l'accent sur ce dernier. Ibn al-Qayyim observe que le fait d'être agréé par Dieu découle du fait de L'agréer, tandis qu'Ibn Sa'di et d'autres comprennent le grand succès comme le salut du feu et l'entrée au Paradis.

Les commentateurs expliquent que ce verset conclut le récit de l'entretien entre Dieu et Jésus, fils de Marie, face aux chrétiens. Son sens est que la royauté des cieux, de la terre et de tout ce qu'ils contiennent appartient à Dieu seul, de sorte que ni Jésus ni sa mère ne peuvent être des divinités, car ils font partie de ce qu'Il possède. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi et Ibn 'Atiyya y voient une réponse à la prétention chrétienne, par laquelle Dieu s'élève au-dessus de ce qu'on Lui attribue ; ils ajoutent que Sa puissance embrasse toute chose, qu'Il peut faire périr comme Il a créé. Abu al-Su'ud et Abu Hayyan notent que l'emploi de « mā » au lieu de « man » est une généralisation qui, selon les uns, respecte la règle générale et, selon d'autres, marque l'infériorité de ceux qu'on dit divins, ou encore signifie que toutes les créatures sont soumises. Al-Razi et al-Qurtubi relient la clôture de la sourate à ses grands thèmes : la loyauté envers les engagements, la souveraineté divine et la responsabilité. Une partie des exégètes, dont Ibn 'Atiyya, envisage aussi que le verset s'adresse au Prophète et à sa communauté. Tous s'accordent sur l'exclusivité de la royauté divine et sur la puissance absolue de Dieu.
en: God commands the believers to fulfil their contracts, meaning to honour the covenants they have made with their Lord and with one another. He then declares lawful to them the grazing livestock, camels, cattle and sheep and goats, except what is recited to them as forbidden, such as carrion, blood and pork. Hunting is prohibited while they are in the state of ihram. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi read the word contracts broadly, covering oaths of faith, religious obligations and commercial or marriage agreements, while Qatada links it to the alliances of the pre-Islamic period and Ibn Zayd lists five kinds of contract. On the meaning of the lawful beasts, most commentators take the three domestic species, whereas Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar include the unborn foetus found dead in a slaughtered mother. The exegetes agree that hunting is forbidden to the pilgrim in ihram and, according to several, to those within the sacred precinct. Al-Tabari holds that the exception concerns forbidden meat, while others tie it to the ban on hunting. The closing phrase states that God decrees what He wills, and no one may question His judgement. Later in the surah, Ibn Kathir and others report that the prohibition on violating the sacred rites, the sacred month, the offerings and the garlands, and on obstructing those who come to the Sacred House, has in part been abrogated according to the majority, notably by the verse of the sword.

This verse forbids believers from violating the sacred symbols of God's religion: they must not make lawful the fighting in the sacred months, nor violate the offering animals or their garlands, nor harm those who head to the Sacred House seeking bounty and the pleasure of their Lord. Once they have left the state of ihram, hunting is permitted. The hatred of a people who barred them from the Sacred Mosque must not drive them to wrongdoing; rather, they should help one another in righteousness and piety, and not in sin and aggression. The commentators explain that the symbols are the rites of the pilgrimage, according to Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, while others understood them as God's prohibitions and obligations, as Ata and al-Hasan said. As for the sacred months, most take them as the four inviolable months, while some restrict the phrase to Rajab or Dhu al-Qa'da. All agree that the offering is livestock sent to the Sacred House, and that the garlands marked it as such. The meaning of the garlands divides scholars: Ibn Abbas took them to be the garlanded offerings themselves, while Mujahid, Ata and Mutarrif took them to be strips of bark from the sanctuary trees that people wore for safety. On abrogation, Ibn Jarir held that the sacred month, the garlands and the safe passage of polytheists were abrogated, while al-Hasan and Abu Maysara held that nothing in the chapter was abrogated. Ibn Kathir and most scholars treat the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months as abrogated, while others keep it for initiating battle only. Most agree that the command to hunt after leaving ihram is a permission. Finally, the reading of the particle as conditional, with a kasra, is favoured by Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr, while the others read it as causal; Ibn Jarir preferred the latter since the sura was revealed after Hudaybiyya.

This verse forbids believers to eat carrion, blood, pork, what is slaughtered in the name of other than God, the strangled, the beaten to death, the fallen, the gored, and what a predator has eaten, except what you slaughter while it still has life in it. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the exception to cover all these categories, while Malik, in one of his opinions, restricts it to animals not yet mortally finished. It also forbids what is sacrificed on the naṣb, the stones set up for worship, and seeking knowledge of one's fortune with the arrows called azlam, which al-Qurtubi and al-Razi regard as claiming knowledge of the unseen and as wickedness. Most commentators hold that the words that today I have perfected your religion were revealed on the day of Arafat during the Farewell Pilgrimage. Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi take the perfection to mean the completion of duties and limits, whereas Qatada and Ibn Jubayr take it to mean that no polytheist would perform the pilgrimage with the Muslims. The verse ends by permitting the one forced by severe hunger to eat of these prohibited things without deliberately inclining to sin, for God is forgiving and merciful.

This verse answers the Muslims' question about what is lawful for them to eat. The answer is that good things are permitted, meaning what sound natures do not find repugnant and what no text forbids, and that game caught by trained hunting animals is also lawful. The commentators give several occasions of revelation: the killing of dogs in Medina, or the question of 'Adi ibn Hatim and Zayd al-Khayl about hunting with dogs and falcons. All agree that a trained dog, released with the name of God invoked, makes its catch lawful. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and most exegetes include every trained predatory beast and bird, while Ibn 'Umar, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi restrict the verse to dogs. On whether the hunter may eat what the animal has begun to eat, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', al-Sha'bi and Abu Hanifa say no, since the animal held the prey for itself, whereas Salman, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ibn 'Umar and Abu Hurayra allow eating the remainder. Ibn Kathir reports a reconciliation: if the dog eats immediately after catching, the meat is forbidden, but if the hunter waited and the dog ate out of hunger, it does no harm. Most scholars hold that invoking God's name at release is required, though they debate whether it is obligatory. The verse closes with a call to fear God, since His reckoning is swift.

The commentators explain that on this day God made the good things lawful, meaning what is pleasant and not forbidden. According to most of them, the food of the People of the Book, which refers to their slaughtered animals, is permitted to Muslims, and Muslim food is permitted to them. Ibn Abbas and several early scholars allowed the meat of Arab Christians, whereas Ali, Ibn Umar and others forbade it when they invoked a name other than God's; the majority therefore restricted the general permission to slaughter with the invocation of God's name, as other verses require. As for the chaste women mentioned, opinions differ: Mujahid and most jurists understood them as free women, so that a non-Muslim slave woman is excluded, while al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi understood them as chaste women and permitted marriage to a slave woman of the Book. Ibn Abbas forbade marrying women of enemy lands, a view the majority did not share. All agree that the dowry must be paid and that the marriage must be lawful and open, neither debauchery nor secret liaisons. On the meaning of disbelieving in faith, views vary: God, the rules of Islam, declaring the forbidden lawful, or the Qur'an; according to most, the loss of good deeds applies only if one dies in disbelief.

The commentators on the ablution and dry-ablution verse (al-Ma'ida 5:6) explain that it commands believers, when rising to pray, to wash the face, the hands up to the elbows, to wipe the head, and to wash the feet up to the ankles, with full purification required for one who is in major ritual impurity. If water cannot be found, due to illness, travel, or after a minor or major impurity, one performs tayammum with clean earth, wiping the face and hands. They stress that God does not intend hardship and that these rulings are a mercy that calls for gratitude. There is broad agreement that the command is addressed to one who is in a state of minor impurity, that renewing ablution for every prayer is not obligatory, and that earth substitutes for water when water is unavailable. They differ on whether the elbows and ankles are included in the washing: most include them out of caution, while Zufar and Dawud exclude them. On wiping the head, Malik requires all of it, al-Shafi'i requires the least amount that counts as wiping, and Abu Hanifa requires a quarter. As for the feet, most scholars and the established Sunna require washing, while some, including Ibn 'Abbas, held that wiping is enough, and they explained the reading in the genitive by the principle of juxtaposition or by wiping over leather socks. They also disagree on intention, the order of the body parts, and continuity, which the majority considers required. For tayammum, the accepted view is a single strike on the earth with the wiping of the face and hands, and the earth must be clean. Many report that the verse was revealed during the expedition of al-Muraysi' when 'A'isha's necklace was lost.

In this verse God calls on the believers to remember the favour He has bestowed on them, namely guidance to Islam, and the covenant they made with Him when they said, "We hear and we obey." He then commands them to fear Him, reminding them that He knows what the hearts conceal. Most commentators, including Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi, identify this covenant as the pledge of allegiance the believers gave the Prophet, to hear and obey in ease and hardship, in what they love and what they dislike. Some link it to the pledge at al-'Aqaba or the pledge of Ridwan. Mujahid instead sees it as the covenant taken from the descendants of Adam when they were brought forth from his loins. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari consider the first view more probable and better suited to the context. Al-Razi and al-Samarqandi also mention rational and revealed proofs, a view favoured by most theologians. For the commentators, recalling the favour and the pact obliges the believers to keep their word, and piety covers both what is shown and what is hidden. Some connect the verse to the command to be just that follows, others to the opening of the surah on fulfilling contracts, and others mention an occasion involving a plot against the Prophet. Most, however, stress faithfulness to the pledge and fear of God.

In this verse God commands the believers to stand firm for Him, to bear witness with justice, and not to let hatred of a people push them away from fairness. They must act justly toward friend and foe alike, since justice is closer to piety. The commentators agree on the plain sense: justice must be observed in speech, judgment and testimony, with relatives as with adversaries. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress that this applies even to unbelievers and forbids transgression born of anger. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see an added emphasis: if justice is owed to God's enemies, it is owed all the more to believers. On the occasion of revelation, the reports differ. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi relate that it concerns the Jews of Banu al-Nadir or Khaybar who plotted to kill the Prophet when he came to ask their help with a blood-money payment; al-Hasan links it to a Quraysh plot, while Ibn 'Abbas and others connect it to the polytheists who barred access to the Sacred Mosque. Al-Razi notes that the verse may be general or limited to unbelievers. Ibn Kathir adds that justice is closer to piety than injustice in every case, and reminds that God knows well what people do. The verse ends with the promise of forgiveness and a great reward for believers who do good deeds, and a warning for those who disbelieve.

This verse states that God has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds forgiveness of their sins and a great reward, which most commentators identify with Paradise. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that forgiveness means covering past sins and sparing punishment for them, while the great reward is an additional gift whose extent no one can measure. Al-Razi adds that the promise itself is stronger than naming its object, since God never breaks His word, and that it brings comfort at the hour of death and through the trials of the grave and the Day of Judgment. On the grammar, opinions differ. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud treat the phrase "for them is forgiveness" as explaining the omitted object of the verb "promised", whereas al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi take the promise to be like a saying, or the whole sentence to be what is promised. Al-Qurtubi also reports, from al-Hasan, a reading in which the promised content is implied. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Mahalli present both possibilities. On the meaning of forgiveness, al-Mawardi and al-Razi link it to the erasing of bad deeds. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di stress that the reward comes from God's mercy and not from deeds alone. Commentators also connect the verse to the one before it, which urges justice and piety, and to the one after it, which describes the fate of the disbelievers. Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that the verb "promise" is used for good as well as for evil, as another verse about the hypocrites shows.

This part of the verse states that those who disbelieved in God's oneness, broke His covenants and denied His signs and proofs brought by the messengers are the people of the Blazing Fire, meaning they will remain in it. The commentators agree that this threat balances the promise given to the righteous believers just before, so the Quran combines encouragement with warning. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qurtubi explain that the phrase 'companions of' indicates lasting attachment, al-Razi takes it as clear proof that the disbelievers abide in Hell forever, while Ibn Sa'di understands it as the bond between one companion and another. The immediate context is a call to justice and piety. Regarding the following verse, which recalls a divine favour, the scholars differ on its occasion. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes report that it refers to the plot of the Banu al-Nadir, who planned to kill the Prophet by dropping a stone on him when he came to ask their help with the blood money of the two Amiris. Others, including al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Ashur, relate the episode of the Bedouin who drew the Prophet's sword under a tree during the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa'. Qatada connects it to the prayer of fear, and some to a poisoned meal. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi mention these accounts without deciding between them.

In this verse God asks the believers to remember His favour when a people wanted to stretch out their hands against them, to harm or kill them, and He held those hands back. He then urges them to fear God and to rely on Him alone. The commentators agree on the general meaning: recognising the blessing of divine protection, then practising piety and trust in God. The occasion of revelation, however, is widely disputed. The majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi, report that it concerns the plot of the Banu al-Nadir to kill the Prophet, who had come to ask their help with a blood-money payment, and that Gabriel warned him. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir support this by pointing to the following verses about Jewish treachery. Others, such as al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, relate the story of the Bedouin who drew the Prophet's sword under a tree, which al-Bukhari also mentions, or the plan to attack the Muslims during the noon prayer at Dhat al-Riqa, which for Qatada led to the prayer of fear, a view repeated by al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi. Al-Razi presents several of these accounts without deciding between them. Ibn 'Ashur holds that the verse refers to a group known to the early Muslims, probably at the battle of the Confederates, and finds the specific narratives unconvincing. Abu Hayyan and al-Razi stress that the verse mainly affirms God's general protection against enemies. On doctrine, Ibn 'Uthaymin notes that trust in God does not exclude taking the necessary means, while Ibn Sa'di treats it as a duty of the heart, in line with the broad agreement on the central place of reliance on God.

This verse recalls the covenant God made with the Children of Israel, and the twelve chiefs (nuqaba') chosen from their tribes to stand as guarantors for their people. God promises them his support if they establish prayer, give zakat, believe in his messengers, support them and make a good loan to God; he will then remove their misdeeds and admit them to gardens with rivers flowing beneath. Whoever disbelieves after this has strayed from the right path. The commentators broadly agree that the covenant means obeying God's commands, and that prayer and almsgiving were enjoined on earlier nations as well as on this community. They differ on the meaning of naqib: Qatada takes it as a witness over his people, Mujahid, al-Rabi' and Abu 'Ubayda as a guarantor or trustee, and al-Zajjaj as one who probes the affairs of his people. On 'azzara, al-Hasan and Mujahid read it as giving help, while Abu 'Ubayda reads it as honouring; al-Tabari favours the sense of help, citing another verse in al-Fath where the word means to honour. Several reports describe the chiefs sent to scout the giants of Syria, their discouragement of their people, and their breaking of the pact, except Yusha' ibn Nun and Kalib ibn Yafunna. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Qayyim reject the Israelite accounts of 'Awj ibn 'Unuq, and al-Alusi considers the most plausible view to be that he was a remnant of the people of 'Ad. God's presence is generally understood as support and aid, and most commentators address these words to all the Children of Israel, while al-Rabi' applies them to the chiefs alone.

The commentators explain that this verse speaks of the Children of Israel who broke the covenant God had made with them, and that their punishment was to be cast away from mercy and to have hardened hearts. They distorted the words of Scripture and forgot a portion of what they had been commanded, and their treachery ceased only among a few of them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi agree that the curse means being distanced from mercy, and that the hardness of heart means a rigidity that exhortation cannot soften. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see it rather as divine abandonment that denies these hearts God's favours. The reading qasiyya, followed by Hamza and al-Kisa'i, is taken by al-Tabari as stronger in blame, while others connect it with debased coins, meaning faith mixed with disbelief. As for the distortion of words, Ibn Abbas understands it as false interpretation of the Book, while others speak of changes to the text itself, including what concerns the signs of the Prophet ﷺ. On the word khaina, Qatada takes it as treachery itself, Mujahid as a treacherous group, and some as a plot against the Prophet ﷺ. Regarding the pardon commanded, Qatada and most scholars regard it as abrogated by the verse of fighting in al-Tawba; al-Tabari keeps it valid for those who had a treaty and paid the poll tax, and Ibn Ashur reads it as a call to noble conduct that does not contradict the command to fight. The exception of a few is taken by most to refer to Abdullah ibn Salam and his companions.

This verse states that God also took a covenant from those who called themselves Christians, as He had from earlier people, but they forgot a considerable part of what they had been reminded of, so God stirred enmity and hatred among them. Al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir understand this as the divisions among Christian sects, namely the Nestorians, Jacobites and Melkites, each of which denounced the others. Al-Tabari prefers the view of al-Rabi' ibn Anas that the pronoun refers to the Christians alone, while Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi, in another report, include both Jews and Christians. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Razi explain the verb 'aghrayna' as making things stick together, like glue. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan note that the name 'Christians' reflects their claim to support God rather than their actual conduct. Al-Hasan al-Basri adds that the name comes from their own saying. Al-Tabari also cites al-Nakha'i, who explains the enmity as arising from doctrinal differences and disputes over religion. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di see the verse ending as a warning that God will inform them of what they did.

This verse addresses the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, announcing that Our Messenger Muhammad ﷺ has come to them. He makes clear much of what they were concealing from their Scripture, such as the ruling on stoning and the description of the Prophet, and passes over many matters that need not be mentioned. The verse then describes what has come from Allah as a light and a clear Book, through which Allah guides whoever seeks His pleasure to the paths of peace and brings people out of darkness into light. The commentators agree that the address includes both Jews and Christians, that the Messenger is Muhammad ﷺ, and that the concealment includes the mention of the Prophet and the ruling of stoning, as reported from Ibn 'Abbas by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi. On the meaning of light, they differ: Qatada and al-Zajjaj take it to be the Prophet, others take it to be Islam, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Jubba'i take it to be the Qur'an, which dispels the darkness of polytheism and doubt. On the paths of peace, al-Hasan and as-Suddi understand them as the religion of Allah or Islam, while others understand them as the ways of safety or the path to Paradise. Ibn 'Ashur notes that pardon here may mean overlooking ignorance. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi stress that the revelation of hidden matters by an unlettered Prophet is itself a proof of his prophethood. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that the title People of the Book serves to establish the proof against them rather than to honour them.

This passage of Surat al-Ma'ida explains that God guides through the Clear Book, the Qur'an, those who seek His good pleasure, along the paths of peace, meaning the ways of safety and deliverance from God's punishment. He brings them out of the darkness of disbelief and association into the light of faith, by His permission, and guides them to the straight path, which is the true religion. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, agree that the Clear Book is the Qur'an, the straight path is Islam, the darkness is disbelief and the light is faith. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi report from al-Hasan and al-Suddi that al-Salam is one of God's names, so His paths are the laws He established for His servants, whereas al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kathir take it as a verbal noun meaning safety, so the paths are the ways that preserve one from danger and punishment. Ibn 'Abbas explains the paths of peace as the religion of Islam. As for the pronoun in 'by it', some take it to refer to the Book, others to the Messenger, or to Islam. On the word 'good pleasure', al-Tabari understands it as acceptance and praise, while others understand it as the opposite of anger. Al-Razi adds that whoever seeks God's good pleasure is the one who pursues the religion through reflection and reasoning, not the one who merely follows the traditions of his forefathers. For 'by His permission', al-Tabari sees divine support and the making of faith beloved, while Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn see it as God's will. The commentators do not rule between these explanations, which they present as complementary.

This verse declares that those who say God is the Messiah, son of Mary, have disbelieved, and it answers them with an argument from reason: if God willed to destroy the Messiah, his mother and everyone on earth, no one could prevent Him, so how could such a being be God? The commentators agree that the target is a Christian group holding that God dwells in or unites with the Messiah, though they differ on its identity. Ibn 'Abbas and those who follow him take them to be the Christians of Najran, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir identify them with the Ya'qubiyya, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi note that the verse may be pointing to the logical consequence of their doctrine even if no one stated it outright; al-Razi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn 'Ashur follow a similar reading and detail the nature of this belief. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir stress that the Messiah is a created human like the other sons of Adam, and that God alone is the Living who does not die. On the phrase 'He creates what He wills,' most exegetes cite the creation of Adam without father or mother, of Eve from Adam, and of Jesus from a mother without a father, all creation depending solely on God's will. As for the dual 'what is between them,' al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi explain it refers to the two kinds of created things, supported by a line of the poet al-Ra'i. Most commentators present these readings without deciding between the views on the exact origin of the belief in question.

This verse reports the claim of Jews and Christians that they are the 'sons of God and His beloved.' The commentators explain that sonship here usually means closeness, tenderness and standing before God rather than literal begetting. God answers that a father does not punish his son, nor does a beloved punish the one he loves; yet they themselves acknowledge that God punishes them for their sins, which refutes their claim. He then reminds them that they are only human beings, among the creatures He has made; He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, the dominion of the heavens and the earth belongs to Him alone, and to Him is the final return. The commentators agree that the verse rejects the claim and affirms the equality of people before God. They differ on the origin of the claim: according to Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Ishaq, some Jews said it in reply to the Prophet's warning; according to al-Suddi, the Jews believed God had revealed to Israel that his firstborn son would be punished forty days in the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read it as referring to the followers of Uzayr and the Messiah, al-Hasan takes it to mean closeness to God, and Ibn Kathir holds that the Jews distorted a passage of their scripture. Al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Kathir point out that the verse implies God does not punish those He loves, citing a hadith of Anas, while others take the punishment to be worldly, such as transformation or exile. The commentators note that God's will is tied to wisdom and causes, and that forgiveness and punishment depend on faith and disbelief.

God addresses the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, and tells them that His messenger Muhammad ﷺ has come to make things clear to them during a period when revelation had lapsed and no messengers had come, so that they cannot say on the Day of Judgment that no bringer of good news or warner ever came to them. A bringer of good news and a warner have now come, and God is capable of all things. The commentators agree that fatra means a gap or pause between messengers, but they differ on its length. Abu Uthman al-Nahdi, Salman al-Farisi, Muqatil and Wahb ibn Munabbih say six hundred years, Qatada is reported with five hundred and sixty years in one account, and al-Dahhak gives about four hundred and thirty-four years. Ibn Kathir considers six hundred years the best-known view and reconciles the figures by the difference between solar and lunar years. On the phrase 'an taqulu', the Basran grammarians read it as 'lest you say', while the Kufans read it as 'so that you do not say'; this is a grammatical debate that does not change the overall meaning. Most exegetes explain that the verse answers Jews who denied that God had sent any book or messenger after Moses, as Ibn Abbas reports. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it mainly as a favour to the People of the Book, who received a messenger when they most needed one. Ibn Atiyya and al-Tabari hold that the object of 'yubayyinu' is left out so as to cover everything they need in religious matters, and al-Razi notes that earlier laws had been distorted, mixing truth with falsehood. Bashir is one who gives good news of reward to the obedient, and nadhir one who warns the disobedient of punishment. The verse closes with God's power, reminding that He can send messengers, and reward or punish.

Moses reminds his people of God's favours: He raised prophets among them, made them kings, and gave them what He had given no other people. He then urges them to enter the holy land that God has ordained for them and warns them not to turn back. The commentators agree that the address is from Moses to the Israelites and aims to rouse them to fight and prepare their hearts. On the "prophets", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand those who succeeded one another among them, while Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi take them to be the seventy men Moses chose, and al-Mawardi reports both views. On "kingship", as-Suddi and Ibn 'Atiyya see it as their deliverance from Egyptian enslavement, which made them masters of themselves; Qatada says they were the first to own servants, while al-Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others hold that whoever has a wife, a servant and a house is a king, and ad-Dahhak relates it to a spacious dwelling with flowing water. As for "what He gave no other people", Mujahid and Ibn 'Abbas cite the manna, the quails, the water from the rock and the shading cloud, while others point to the number of prophets among them. The holy land is identified as Jericho by Ibn 'Abbas and as-Suddi, as Mount Sinai and its surroundings by Mujahid, as all of Syria by Qatada, and as Damascus, Palestine and part of Jordan by az-Zajjaj. Al-Tabari notes that some attribute the final "you" to the community of Muhammad, the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Abu Malik, but the majority hold that it is Moses speaking. The passage then recounts the people's refusal because of the giants, the encouragement of Yusha' and Kalib, and the decree that bars the land from them for forty years of wandering.

This verse records Moses telling his people, the Children of Israel, to enter the holy land that God has prescribed for them, and not to turn back on their heels, lest they end up losers. The commentators agree that "holy" means pure or blessed, and that the land is Syria in its broad sense, the dwelling of the prophets. They differ on its exact extent: Mujahid, as reported by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, says it is Mount Sinai and its surroundings; Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd say it is Jericho; al-Kalbi and al-Zajjaj name Damascus, Palestine and part of Jordan; Qatada says all of Syria. On the meaning of "God has written for you", Ibn Ishaq takes it as a gift, al-Suddi as a command, while al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi read it as recorded in the Preserved Tablet. The apparent difficulty of the next verse, "it is forbidden to them", is answered in several ways: the gift was conditional on obedience, the prohibition lasted forty years, or the promise concerned their descendants. Turning back on the heels is read either literally as fleeing from the giants or figuratively as abandoning the faith. Several commentators relay accounts of the giants' enormous size, which Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi regard as Israelite narratives of doubtful reliability. Ibn Kathir also cites the authentic report that at Badr the Companions refused to speak as the people of Moses had spoken to him.

The Quran recounts the response of the Children of Israel to their prophet Moses when he commanded them to enter the Holy Land. They said that a people of giants, the jabbarin, were there, and that they would never enter as long as those people remained, but that they would enter once those people had left. The commentators agree that the jabbar is one who compels others to his will, and that the word derives from the notions of compulsion and mending. They also agree that the Holy Land is the region of Syria, though they differ on its exact location: al-Tabari and al-Baghawi report that Mujahid identified it with Mount Tur and its surroundings, Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd with Jericho, al-Kalbi with Damascus, Palestine and part of Jordan, while Qatada included all of Syria. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the fear arose after Moses sent the twelve chiefs to scout the land, and they returned describing the inhabitants with dread. Only Joshua and Caleb remained faithful and told the people to enter by the gate and to trust in God. Al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy note that the two men spoke out of certainty in God's promise. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya observe that the phrase 'God has written for you' signifies divine decree rather than legal obligation, whereas Ibn Kathir sees it as a promise handed down by the forefathers. Most commentators read the passage as exposing the people's cowardice and their disrespect toward their prophet, whom they addressed by name without a title, and they link it to the forty years of wandering that followed.

According to the commentators, Moses commanded the Children of Israel to enter the Holy Land, but most of them refused in fear, after the scouts reported the great size and fierceness of the giants. Two men among those who feared God, Joshua son of Nun and Caleb, on whom God had bestowed grace, urged their people to enter the city by its gate by surprise, for once inside they would prevail, and they told them to trust in God if they were believers. The commentators report that these two were among the chosen leaders who had kept what they saw secret, telling only Moses, while the rest spread the news and lost heart. The commentators differ on the meaning of 'those who fear'. Qatada, Ibn Abbas and most of the scholars take it to mean fear of God. Others take it to mean fear of the tyrants, or fear of the weakness and cowardice of the Children of Israel. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr read 'yukhafun' (passive), which some take to mean the two men were of the giants who had embraced faith. The Israelites replied that they would not enter as long as the giants were there, and said to Moses: 'Go, you and your Lord, and fight!' Moses then prayed that God separate him from the rebellious people, and God decreed that the land be forbidden to them for forty years, during which they wandered. The commentators cite this episode when al-Miqdad told the Prophet at Badr that they would not say to him what the Children of Israel had said to Moses, but would fight at his side. This is a point on which the commentators agree in presenting it as an example of obedience.

The Qur'an recounts that the Children of Israel, after Moses commanded them to enter the Holy Land and fight its tyrannical inhabitants, boldly refused, saying they would never enter as long as those people were there, and told him: go, you and your Lord, and fight; we will sit here. The commentators read the phrase 'go, you and your Lord' in different ways: al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir treat it as disbelief if it meant literal going, while Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others take it to mean 'may your Lord help you'. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir also mention that 'Lord' may refer to Aaron, Moses' elder brother. Opinions differ on the nature of their offence: many consider it grave disobedience and impiety, others see it as presumption against God and His messenger. Moses disavowed them and asked God to separate him from them; God replied that the land was forbidden to them for forty years, during which they would wander. The scholars agree this was a punishment, and the prohibition on grieving over the wicked was a consolation to Moses. Several report that at Badr and Hudaybiya the Companions answered the Prophet that they would not speak as the Children of Israel had, but would fight alongside him. The two men who encouraged their people are, according to most, Joshua and Caleb, though accounts vary. The passage warns against shrinking from God's command and against cowardice in battle, and shows the consequences of such conduct.

After the Children of Israel refused to enter the Holy Land while its tyrants remained, Moses turned to his Lord, lamenting and disowning their stance: "My Lord, I have no power except over myself and my brother, so separate us from the defiant people." Most commentators understand that only Moses and Aaron obeyed him, and that the request for separation means a judgment between them and the rebels, or their removal from his company. Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya explain that the separation sought is a judgment, and that the words amount to a curse upon the rebels. Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi add that Moses did not fully trust the two men who had urged the people to advance, given their wavering, and so he did not name them. As for the grammar of "and my brother", scholars proposed several readings, as an appositive to "myself", as a conjunction with the pronoun in "I do not possess", or as a nominative, without a decisive ruling.

The commentators agree that the defiant people (al-fasiqin) are those who disobeyed God's command. The reply "go, you and your Lord, and fight" was judged by some to be a statement of disbelief because of its anthropomorphic implication, and by others as disobedience or mockery; Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan lean toward mockery. As for the wandering, Ibn 'Abbas and most exegetes hold it lasted forty years, during which those who had refused did not enter the land, and their children did. Others hold that the prohibition was limited to forty years while the wandering itself had no fixed term. Some say Moses and Aaron were with them without suffering the punishment, others that they were not, and this remains debated.

This passage recounts that when the Israelites refused to enter the holy land, saying 'go you and your Lord and fight, we will sit here,' Moses prayed against them. God replied that the land is forbidden to them for forty years, during which they wander, and told Moses not to grieve over this wicked people. The commentators agree that this prohibition is a decree of deprivation, not a ritual prohibition. They also agree that the Israelites wandered in a small area, walking all day and ending where they had started. They differ on the size of that desert: nine farsakhs according to Ibn 'Abbas, six by twelve farsakhs according to others, thirty according to Muqatil. They also differ on the reach of 'forty years': al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi attach it to the prohibition, so their children later entered with Joshua, while Qatada attaches it to the wandering. Opinions also vary on whether Moses and Aaron were in the desert: some say they were there as a mercy, others that they were not, and Aaron is said to have died there first. Several commentators, including Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur, note that the stories about the giant 'Awj ibn 'Unuq come from unreliable Israelite material. Readers also take from this that trust in God does not excuse taking action, and that rebuking sinners and shunning them should be guided by what is beneficial.

God commands His Messenger ﷺ to recite to his people the account of the two sons of Adam, Habil and Qabil, truthfully. Each offered a sacrifice to God; one was accepted and the other was not. The one whose offering was rejected threatened to kill his brother, who replied that God accepts only from the God-fearing. The commentators, including Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, agree that the two were full brothers, sons of Adam, and that the killer was the first to introduce murder. The accepted offering was the best of the giver's property, while the rejected one was the worst of his produce. The reports say the sign of acceptance was a fire descending to consume the offering, but Ibn Kathir and others note that many of these narrations come from the People of the Book and are not authenticated. Al-Hasan al-Basri held that they were two men from the Children of Israel, but most exegetes, including at-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi, prefer the first view. Most explain the piety in the verse as piety against polytheism, while others take it as general God-consciousness. Habil said he would not raise his hand against his brother out of fear of God; some say he was stronger but refrained out of scruple. A sound hadith states that the unjust killer bears a share of the sin because he was the first to establish killing. The commentators also agree that the raven taught the killer how to bury his brother's body, and that he then regretted not finding the way himself.

This part of the story gives the words of the innocent brother, Habil, to Qabil, who threatened to kill him: he tells him that he will not raise his hand to kill him, and he gives as his reason the fear of God, Lord of the worlds. The commentators agree on the apparent meaning: Habil will not be the first to attack. They differ, however, on why he refused to defend himself, although according to most he was stronger than his brother. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Umar, followed by most, explain that his scrupulous piety prevented him, even though he had the power and the right to resist, a view also taken by Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn 'Atiyya. Al-Hasan and Mujahid hold instead that self-defence was not permitted under that law and that the duty was not to resist whoever wished to kill. As-Samani and al-Qurtubi report that for someone who is about to be killed it is permissible to submit, hoping for the reward, as 'Uthman did. Ar-Razi and Abu Hayyan cite other explanations, including that Habil wanted to remind his brother of the gravity of the crime before he committed it. Ibn Kathir sees the verse as an exhortation and warning addressed to Qabil. He reports, as do many others, that Qabil killed his brother by surprise while he slept. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas about strife, in which he is told to be like the better of Adam's two sons, and ar-Razi cites the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud that the first son of Adam was the first to establish killing. The commentators also differ on the meaning of the following phrase: some say it means that the killer will bear the weight of his crime and his earlier sins, others that it means only that he will suffer the punishment for his killing.

This verse records Habil's words to his brother Qabil, who had threatened to kill him: he will not raise his hand against him, because he fears Allah, Lord of the worlds. He then says he wishes that Qabil bear the sin of killing him together with his earlier sins, and so become one of the people of the Fire, which is the recompense of wrongdoers. Most commentators, including Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and Qatada, understand that Qabil will bear the sin of the murder together with his past sins, and al-Tabari adopts this view, holding that a person does not bear the sin of his victim but only his own. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the phrase as a figure of speech, meaning that the brother would prefer that a sin like the one he would commit by defending himself be borne by the aggressor. Al-Zajjaj links the sin to Qabil's refusal to accept God's decision, which prevented his offering from being accepted. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi hold that the killer shares part of the punishment of the victim, citing the hadith transmitted through Ibn Mas'ud, while others read the wish as a metaphor or as a negation, and Abu Hayyan reports several readings. Al-Razi and others report that Qabil killed his brother and was then seized with remorse after watching a crow bury another crow.

This verse tells how Qabil's soul made the killing of his brother Habil seem easy to him, so he killed him and became one of the losers. The commentators agree that the verb tawwaʿat means to make easy, to encourage or to embellish: al-Tabari and Mujahid speak of encouragement, Qatada of making it look attractive, and Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi also mention facilitation and submission. They also agree that the loss described is twofold. In this life he angered his parents and was left without a brother; in the next life he angered his Lord and deserved the Fire, as Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and al-Samʿani explain. The accounts of how he killed his brother differ. Al-Sudi and Ibn 'Abbas report that he crushed his head with a rock while he slept, while Ibn Jurayj and Mujahid relate that Iblis taught him by crushing the head of a bird between two stones. Al-Tabari does not choose between these reports, and the place of the killing is also disputed, given as Mount Thawr, the peak of Hira, or Basra. Several scholars, including Ibn Kathir, report that God sent a crow to show Qabil how to bury the body. The hadith transmitted by Ibn Mas'ud, that the first son bears a share of every unjust killing because he was the first to set the precedent, is cited by al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir. As for Qabil's state of faith, some say he was an unbeliever and others that he was a sinner; al-Qurtubi holds that he was a disobedient person rather than an unbeliever.

The verse tells how God sent a crow that scratched the ground to show the killer how to bury his brother's body. Seeing this, the killer cried out that he had been unable to be like this crow in covering his brother's corpse, and he became one of the regretful. Most commentators agree that the two men were the sons of Adam by his own loins, Habil and Qabil, and that the killer carried his brother's body for a long time without knowing how to bury it. As to how the crow was sent, Ibn Abbas and Mujahid report that two crows fought and one killed the other, after which the survivor dug a grave and buried it, while al-Asamm and Abu Muslim hold that the crow itself buried a dead crow, and others say it was an angel in the form of a crow. The opinions agree that sawa'a means the corpse or its nakedness, and that the killer's regret concerned the burden he had carried and his own bewilderment rather than the killing itself, which is why it was not a true repentance, though Ibn Abbas says that regret for the killing would have been a repentance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others transmit many reports about the envy that led Qabil to murder, and about the offering of Habil alone being accepted, but several exegetes regard these details as drawn from the stories of the People of the Book and keep to the text itself. Al-Tabari also cites a view from al-Hasan that the two men were Children of Israel, an isolated opinion the majority did not adopt. Many cite the hadith that every unjust killing carries a share of guilt to the first son of Adam, since he was the first to establish killing.

This passage establishes that unjustly taking a human life is an enormous crime. According to the commentators, the prescription given to the Children of Israel is that whoever kills a soul without retaliation or corruption in the land, it is as if he had killed all of mankind, and whoever preserves a soul, by refraining from killing it or rescuing it from ruin, it is as if he had preserved all of mankind. Most commentators agree that the comparison serves to magnify the crime and its gravity, and that the killer of an unjustly slain soul bears a punishment resembling that of one who kills all people, as reported from Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Kathir, and they regard refraining from killing as a form of giving life. Ibn Zayd and Ibn Kathir understand giving life as pardoning the killer by the heirs of the blood, a view al-Hasan also holds, while Mujahid and others explain it as rescuing someone from drowning, fire or destruction. Ibn Abbas, in one report, and Ikrima take the verse to concern killing a prophet or a just ruler and supporting them. Many discuss corruption in the land, citing polytheism, highway robbery and armed brigandage. In the following verse God says that His messengers came to the Children of Israel with clear proofs, yet many of them still transgressed on earth through killing and sin, which the commentators explain as excess in evil and indifference to the gravity of killing. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi draw on the passage for the rules concerning brigands, whose penalty is execution, crucifixion, amputation or banishment, while the commentators differ on the details of these penalties and on whether the wording grants the ruler a choice.

This verse prescribes the punishment for those who wage war against God and His Messenger and spread corruption in the land. Most commentators understand it to refer to highway robbers who terrorize people with weapons, kill, and seize property. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that waging war on God means defying His law and opposing His allies rather than fighting Him directly, and Ibn Kathir notes that the ruling applies generally even though the verse may have had a specific occasion. The reports on the occasion of revelation differ: some tell of men from 'Uraynah and 'Ukl who apostatized, killed a herdsman and drove off camels, while others link the verse to what the Prophet had done to them, either as a later abrogation of that punishment or as a ruling given before the legal limits were set.

Scholars disagree on whether the word "or" makes the penalties optional. Ibn 'Abbas in one report, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i and Abu Thawr hold that the ruler may choose whichever penalty he judges best. Ibn 'Abbas in another report, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad hold that the penalties are graded by the offence: whoever kills and takes property is killed and crucified, whoever only kills is killed, whoever only takes property loses a hand and the opposite foot, and whoever only spreads fear is exiled. Malik grants the ruler discretion while preferring the lighter penalty when no one was killed.

As for exile, al-Tabari takes it to mean banishment from one town to another with imprisonment until repentance appears, Abu Hanifa understands it as detention, and al-Shafi'i as continued pursuit. Repentance before capture removes the prescribed penalty, but the scholars differ on the victims' rights: al-Shafi'i holds that they remain, while Malik holds that they lapse except in cases of bloodshed, with further nuances.

This verse grants an exception to the highwaymen and corrupters on earth: whoever repents before being captured is spared the penalties for the rights of God listed in the preceding verse, namely execution, crucifixion, cutting off the opposite hand and foot, or exile, and is promised God's forgiveness and mercy. The commentators differ on who the exception covers. Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid and al-Hasan take the verse to concern polytheists, whose conversion before capture removes the penalty, while al-Shafi'i, Malik, Abu Thawr and most jurists hold that it concerns Muslim brigands, so that repentance before capture removes only the rights of God and not human rights. Al-Sha'bi reports that Ali ibn Abi Talib granted safe conduct to Haritha ibn Badr, who repented before being seized, pardoning him for blood and property. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd and Ibn Ajlan considered the penalties to have applied to specific individuals, while al-Awza'i judged them to apply to others. On property and bloodshed, Malik and al-Awza'i held that the penitent is not pursued for past acts unless stolen goods identifiable as belonging to someone are found in his possession, whereas al-Shafi'i maintained that human rights are not lifted by repentance. Repentance after capture does not remove the punishment, a point on which there is broad agreement. The common thread is that sincere repentance shown before justice reaches the offender opens the door to pardon.

In this verse God commands believers to be mindful of Him, meaning to guard against His punishment by doing what He commands and avoiding what He forbids, to seek a means of drawing near to Him, and to strive in His path so that they may prosper. Ibn Kathir reports that the exegetes agree that wasila means nearness to God through obedience and what pleases Him, a view attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu Wa'il, al-Hasan, Qatada, 'Ata', al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. Al-Shinqiti adds that this nearness can only be reached by following what the Prophet brought. Al-Tabari and Ibn Zayd, as cited by Ibn al-Jawzi, understand it as love, that is, making oneself beloved to God. Ibn 'Abbas is also reported to have taken it to mean need, quoting a line of 'Antara, and al-Shinqiti holds that asking is itself part of worship. Many commentators also note that wasila names a high rank in Paradise, which the Prophet hopes to attain according to hadiths cited by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, whereas Ibn 'Ashur takes the word here in its general sense of nearness. Striving is named after fearing God because it is a burden on the soul, as al-Razi observes about both avoiding what is forbidden and performing what is required. As for the verses about disbelievers, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take them to say that ransom will not be accepted on the Day of Judgment, and that their wish to leave the Fire is only a longing. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir report a disagreement: some apply the statement that they will not leave the Fire to sinful believers, as transmitted from Jabir, while others, including Ibn 'Abbas answering Nafi' ibn al-Azraq, restrict it to disbelievers.

This verse states that those who disbelieve, even if they owned everything on earth and the same again and wished to ransom themselves with it from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, would not have it accepted, and a painful torment awaits them. Commentators read this as an image meant to show that punishment is unavoidable and that there is no way out, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain. A hadith narrated from Anas is often cited: the disbeliever will be asked whether he would ransom himself with the gold of the whole earth, he will say yes, and he will be told that something far easier had been asked of him. The exegetes agree that the verse concerns unbelievers, that ransom is of no use once punishment has come, and that they will not leave the Fire. They differ, however, on sinning believers. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that some scholars cite this verse to argue that God will bring out of the Fire those who sincerely say there is no god but God, since the eternal punishment is restricted to disbelievers. Al-Zamakhshari rejects this reading, attributed to Ikrima, and calls it a fabrication. On the preceding verse, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani explain that the wasila is drawing near to God through obedience, while Ibn Juzayy takes it as anything by which one draws closer, whether good deeds or supplication, and Ibn Kathir adds hadiths describing the wasila as a supreme rank in Paradise reserved for the Prophet. Taken together, the commentaries call for piety and obedience, since salvation comes neither through wealth nor through ransom.

This verse states that on the Day of Resurrection the disbelievers will wish to leave the Fire, yet they will never leave it, and their punishment is lasting. The commentators agree on the overall meaning but differ on the nature of this wish. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi, take it as a desire or longing in the heart. Al-Hasan al-Basri, reported by Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi, holds that the flames lift them towards the gates of the Fire, where they truly seek to get out before being pushed back; al-Jubba'i reads the word as wishing, and others say they nearly come out. Several scholars, including Ibn 'Abbas as transmitted by al-Tabari, say the verse concerns only the disbelievers, a view supported by Jabir ibn 'Abdullah and a hadith in Muslim. Al-Razi notes that some Sunni scholars cite the verse to argue that those who profess monotheism will eventually leave the Fire, while al-Zamakhshari rejects the report of the dispute between Nafi' ibn al-Azraq and Ibn 'Abbas as a fabrication, and al-Alusi defends it. The word muqim means lasting and enduring, neither ceasing nor changing, according to al-Tabari and Abu Hayyan. Ibn 'Uthaymin maintains that the Fire itself is everlasting, citing several verses. The verse also shows that ransom is impossible: even if one offered the whole earth and as much again, it would not be accepted, as Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari note from a hadith of Anas.

This verse prescribes the punishment for the male and female thief: their hands are to be cut off as a recompense for what they have earned and as an exemplary deterrent from God. Most commentators understand the right hand, cut at the wrist, and Ibn Mas'ud's reading "their right hands" is noted. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes hold that the ruling is limited by conditions, chiefly that the stolen property be worth at least a quarter of a dinar and be taken from a secure place; this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Malik and Ahmad. Abu Hanifa sets the threshold at ten dirhams, while Dawud, the Kharijites and al-Hasan al-Basri hold that the penalty applies to any theft, small or large. These positions rest on hadiths reported through Aisha, Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas. Commentators also differ on repeat offences: the majority cut the left foot on a second theft, Ali and others prefer imprisonment, and al-Shafi'i allows amputation of a hand and foot on the third and fourth. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that most scholars do not consider repentance to lift the punishment, which concerns the relationship with God, whereas Ata' and one opinion of al-Shafi'i hold that repentance before capture removes it. Ibn Kathir recounts the Makhzumite woman whose hand was cut despite Usama's intercession, and who later repented well. Finally, the restitution of the stolen goods is debated: al-Shafi'i and Ahmad require it, Abu Hanifa does not, and Malik distinguishes according to the thief's means. The closing verses affirm that God owns the heavens and the earth, punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills.

This verse states that whoever repents after committing theft, and sets his conduct right through genuine remorse, giving up the sin and returning what he took or seeking the victim's forgiveness, will have his repentance accepted by God, for God is Forgiving and Merciful. The commentators agree that sincere repentance benefits the person before his Lord. They differ on whether it removes the worldly punishment. Al-Tabari reports that Mujahid took the prescribed penalty itself to be the repentance, and Ibn Kathir, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi hold that the amputation is not lifted by repentance, since it also concerns the right of the victim, a view shared by al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud. Ibn al-Arabi, cited by Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur, argues that the brigand stands on his own power while the thief is in the hands of the Muslims. Al-Mawardi reports that 'Ata' and one of al-Shafi'i's opinions hold that repentance before arrest removes the amputation. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur cite the account of the Makhzumite woman who repented after her hand was cut off. Al-Razi notes that the mention of forgiveness and mercy may, for some early scholars, imply the lifting of the penalty, while others confine it to the hereafter. These questions remain open, and the commentators record their views without settling them.

This verse states that God holds absolute sovereignty over the heavens and the earth: He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and He is capable of all things. The commentators read the question "Do you not know?" as a way of affirming a fact, addressed either to the Prophet ﷺ or to anyone able to understand. They agree that this power means God shows no favouritism based on kinship or descent, so no one can claim immunity by virtue of being God's child, as al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi explain. Most say that punishment is mentioned before forgiveness because the context concerns legal penalties and the theft precedes the repentance, as al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Juzayy and al-Baydawi note. The meaning of punishment and forgiveness is disputed. Al-Kalbi and al-Suddi, along with one report from Ibn Abbas, take it as punishment for those who die in disbelief and forgiveness for those who repent of it, while another report from Ibn Abbas distinguishes minor sins that are punished from major sins that are forgiven. Others, including al-Tabari and al-Razi, understand it as happening in this world: killing, transformation or sinking on one side, repentance and deliverance on the other. Ibn Kathir, who links the verse to the amputation of the thief's hand, records the disagreements over the minimum value of stolen goods and the requirement of a protected place, without settling them. Al-Razi stresses that this power is bound by no constraint, while several scholars note that the verse has been used in wider theological debates about divine freedom.

The verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ and forbids him to grieve over those who race into disbelief: hypocrites who say with their mouths that they believe while their hearts do not, and Jews who listen eagerly to falsehood and to others who never came to him, distorting words after they had grasped their meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others relate that the revelation first concerns a Jewish man and woman who committed adultery. Their scholars had replaced stoning with flogging and blackening the face, then sent them to the Prophet, agreeing to accept his ruling if it matched their wish and to reject it otherwise. He ordered stoning as the Torah prescribes, a report transmitted by Ibn Umar in al-Bukhari and Muslim. Other reports place the revelation in a blood feud between Qurayza and Nadir, or name hypocrites, Ibn Sawriya or Abu Lubaba, but al-Tabari favours the adultery account.
