On the meaning of God's willing someone's trial, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi cite misguidance, punishment or exposure, while the Mu'tazilites, as al-Zamakhshari reports, understand it as God withholding His favour. Sunni commentators see the purification of the heart as tied to God's own will, while others read it as a judgment on the uselessness of divine grace. The following verse describes these Jews as avid for lies and unlawful gain, and leaves the Prophet free to judge between them or turn away. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir see that choice as abrogated by the command to judge by what God has revealed, whereas al-Qurtubi upholds it. In sum, disgrace in this world and a great punishment in the next are announced for those whose hearts God has not chosen to purify.

This verse describes the Jews as those who listen eagerly to falsehood and devour unlawful gain. It leaves the Prophet ﷺ, when they come to him for judgement, the choice between judging between them or turning away from them, and states that if he turns away they cannot harm him in the least, while if he judges he must do so with justice, for God loves the just. The commentators broadly agree that suht means unlawful gain, with bribery in judgement the gravest form; Ibn Mas'ud, Ali, Umar and Ibn Abbas list further kinds such as the wage of a prostitute, the price of a dog and the fee of a soothsayer. On the scope of the choice, opinions differ: al-Tabari, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Ata' and Qatada hold that it remains valid and is left to the judge, whereas Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Hasan and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz consider it abrogated by the verse 'Judge between them by what God has revealed'. Others restrict the option to non-protected allies, and al-Shafi'i inclines to the obligation to judge between dhimmis who request it. The occasions of revelation reported include the stoning of a Jewish couple guilty of adultery and a dispute over blood-money between Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayza; Ibn Kathir suggests both circumstances may have coincided. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the option to remain valid as the more apparent view.

This verse expresses God's wonder at the Jews, who ask the Prophet ﷺ to judge between them although they have the Torah, which contains God's judgment, and who then turn away from his ruling after accepting to be judged by him. Al-Tabari reads it as a rebuke to the Jews addressed through the Prophet: if they abandon the judgment of the Torah, which they confess to be true, they are all the more guilty of abandoning the judgment of the Prophet whose prophethood they deny, and those who do this are not believers. Ibn 'Abbas, as-Suddi and Qatada explain that God's judgment in the Torah is stoning, or God's clarification of a dispute over a killing among them; al-Mawardi also reports that it may mean retaliation. Most commentators tell of two Jewish adulterers whom the Prophet ﷺ had stoned after the Torah confirmed this punishment, while others relate a dispute over blood-money between the tribes of Banu Nadir and Banu Qurayza. Az-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan see the question as an expression of astonishment at their appeal to a judge they do not believe in, and Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a reproach implying they do not truly seek justice but what suits their desires. Ar-Razi and al-Baydawi understand the verse as denying that they truly believe in the Torah or in Moses, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress their inconsistency and their pursuit of concessions rather than truth.

These verses state that God sent down the Torah, containing guidance and light, and that the prophets who had submitted to God, followed by the godly masters and scholars of the Children of Israel, judged the Jews by it, since they were entrusted with God's Book and were its witnesses. God commands their scholars to fear Him rather than people, and not to sell His signs for a small price. The commentators agree that the verses primarily address Jews who concealed and altered the ruling on stoning. On judging other than what God revealed, opinions differ: Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus and 'Ata' hold that it is a lesser disbelief that does not expel one from the faith, and that whoever denies the ruling is a disbeliever, while Ibn 'Abbas in one report says whoever acknowledges it but does not apply it is a wrongdoer and an evildoer. Al-Sha'bi assigns the three terms to Muslims, Jews and Christians respectively, while al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i take them as general. Al-Tabari concludes the verses concern disbelieving People of the Book, while their wording is general. The following verse reports that the Torah prescribed retaliation for killing and injuries, and that forgiveness by the victim is an expiation, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and al-Sha'bi, whereas Ibrahim and Mujahid take it as expiation for the forgiver. The commentators also relate occasions of revelation, such as the stoning of the two Jewish adulterers in the Prophet's time and the dispute between Qurayza and Nadir over blood money, while allowing that revelation may have occurred on several occasions. Finally, the verses note that the Gospel also contains guidance and light and command its people to judge by what it contains.

This passage recalls that God had prescribed in the Torah the law of retaliation for the Children of Israel: a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, a tooth for a tooth, and wounds subject to retaliation, meaning the offender receives a punishment matching his offence where equality can be achieved. Commentators agree that this law was imposed on them and that the verse reproaches their distortion of it. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the Banu al-Nadir would kill a man from the Banu Qurayza without retaliation and pay a doubled blood-money, which was an injustice. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd explain that God lightened the burden on this community by instituting the diya, or financial compensation, whereas the Children of Israel had only retaliation or pardon. As for the verse 'whoever forgoes it, it is an expiation for him', there are two main views: Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Amr, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Qatada hold that it is the injured party who, by pardoning, obtains expiation for his sins, and the hadiths cited by al-Tabari and others support this; Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibrahim and al-Sha'bi hold that it is the offender who is absolved when the victim forgives him, the reward of the forgiver being with God. Finally, 'those who do not judge by what God has revealed are the wrongdoers' was explained by Ibn Abbas, Tawus and Ata as a lesser disbelief and a lesser wrong, while others read it as disbelief that takes one out of the religion when judgment is rejected out of conviction, all agreeing that the verse concerns retaliation as well as other rulings.

This verse says that God sent Jesus, son of Mary, after the earlier prophets, to confirm the Torah that came before him, gave him the Gospel, which contains guidance and light, confirms the Torah preceding it, and is a guidance and admonition for the God-fearing. The commentators agree on this general meaning. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Sa'di explain that Jesus affirmed the Torah and called to what it contains. Most of them hold that the Gospel included rulings beyond those of the Torah, but they differ over how much law it contains. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Uthaymin note that the Gospel is mostly admonitions and stories with few legal rulings, and Ibn Uthaymin adds that most of those rulings are taken from the Torah. Ibn Kathir, citing Jesus' words in Surat Al 'Imran, holds that the Gospel abrogated some rulings of the Torah, which he describes as the prevailing view. Al-Tabari, by contrast, holds that Torah rulings not abrogated remain binding. On the repetition of confirming what lies before him, al-Razi explains that the first refers to Jesus and the second to the Gospel, while Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya treat the second as a circumstantial clause. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi add that the Gospel foretells the coming of Muhammad. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that guidance and admonition are specified for the God-fearing because they alone benefit from them. The commentators also discuss the reading of wa-liyahkum as a command or as a purpose clause, without strongly preferring one.

This part of the verse says that God commanded the people of the Gospel to judge by what He revealed in it, and that those who do not judge by what God revealed are the defiantly disobedient, meaning those who leave obedience to God. The commentators differ on how to read the verb. Most readers vocalize it with a sukun on the lam as a command, so the sense is 'and We said: let the people of the Gospel judge by what it contains.' Hamza and al-A'mash read it with a kasra on the lam and a subjunctive verb, giving a purpose sense: 'We gave them the Gospel so that its people might judge by it.' Al-Tabari holds that both readings are close in meaning and both are correct; al-Nahhas also considers them two acceptable readings, while Makki prefers the command form, which the majority use and which fits the warning that follows. Al-Zamakhshari argues that Jesus was bound by the laws of the Torah, but the plain sense of the verse contradicts this; Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir state that the Gospel abrogated some rulings of the Torah, which Ibn Kathir describes as the more widely held view. On the meaning of the command to judge after the Qur'an was revealed, al-Asamm takes it to mean the proofs of Muhammad's prophethood, others take it to mean what was not abrogated, and the majority take it as a warning against altering the Gospel. As for the 'defiantly disobedient', Ibn Zayd understood them as liars, while Ibn Kathir and most others describe them as those who step outside the obedience owed to their Lord. Modern commentators distinguish between rejection out of denial, which amounts to unbelief, and judging out of personal desire, which amounts to sinful deviance.

This verse states that God sent down the Qur'an to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with truth. It confirms the earlier scriptures and watches over them: what is true in them is affirmed, and what is false is rejected. The commentators offer several readings of "muhayminan". Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Kathir take it to mean witness, while Ibn 'Abbas in another transmission, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Hasan take it to mean trustworthy, Ibn Zayd takes it to mean confirmer, and al-Khalil takes it to mean guardian. All agree that the Qur'an abrogates the laws that preceded it. God commands His Prophet to judge between the People of the Book by what God has revealed and not to follow their desires. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi discuss whether this judgement is obligatory or optional: some say this verse abrogates the option given earlier in the chapter, while the majority hold that it is an option, in which case any judgement must follow the revelation. The commentators agree that each community was given a law and a way, shir'a and minhaj, meaning path and custom, while belief in the oneness of God is common to all revelations and only the rulings differ. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that this diversity of laws is a trial from God to test His servants. Believers are therefore urged to race towards good deeds, since the return is to God, who will inform them of what they disputed. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi note that the verse calls for prompt performance of duties, and some draw from it the priority of prayer at its appointed time, while others understand the word khayrat more broadly as all good deeds.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to judge between the People of the Book according to what Allah has revealed, not to follow their desires, and to beware lest they turn him away from part of what was revealed to him. The commentators relate the occasion of revelation: rabbis such as Ka'b ibn Asad, Ibn Suriya and Shas ibn Qays asked the Prophet to rule in their favour in exchange for their belief, and he refused. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya understand the warning as a call to avoid being pulled from a just ruling toward their wishes. On the phrase that Allah wants to afflict them for some of their sins, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi take it as a punishment in this world, which they link to the exile or killing of certain Jewish tribes, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that naming only a part magnifies the gravity of their turning away. On the word fasiqun, Ibn 'Abbas explains it as disbelief, Ibn Zayd as lying and Muqatil as disobedience. Al-Qurtubi discusses whether the verse abrogates the choice given to the Prophet in the earlier verse, noting Ibn al-Arabi's objection that the conditions for abrogation are not met. The commentators agree on the obligation to judge by revealed law and on the danger of following desires.

In this verse God rebukes the Jews who had brought their dispute to the Prophet ﷺ and then turned away from his ruling, seeking instead the 'judgement of ignorance', meaning decisions driven by desire rather than revelation. The question is one of reproach: who judges better than God for a people who have certainty? Al-Tabari and Mujahid identify those addressed as Jews, and al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud agree. The meaning of 'the judgement of ignorance' is more disputed. Al-Wahidi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan relate the occasion of revelation to the quarrel between Banu al-Nadir and Banu Qurayza over blood-money, which the Prophet settled as equal, so the phrase refers to the pre-Islamic practice of ranking victims. Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir widen the sense to any judgement made apart from God's law, and al-Hasan takes it as general. Al-Qurtubi reports that Tawus cited the verse to forbid favouring one child over another in gifts, a view other jurists reject. The readings also differ: Ibn Amir reads 'tabghun' in the second person, the rest 'yabghun'. Ibn Ashur and al-Razi note the interrogative form and the lam of 'li-qawmin', which explains the phrase. Nearly all agree on the core sense: a believer who knows that God's wisdom is perfect never prefers human judgement to His.

This verse forbids believers from taking Jews and Christians as allies and protectors, meaning relying on them, seeking their support, or treating them with the intimacy of close friends. It gives the reason: they support one another, each being an ally of the other against the Muslims. Whoever takes them as allies becomes one of them, and God does not guide the wrongdoers. The commentators agree that the forbidden wilaya is support, alliance and loyalty, not ordinary dealings or neighbourly relations. They differ on the occasion of revelation. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir link it to 'Ubada ibn al-Samit and 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, when the first renounced his alliance with the Jews while the second clung to it out of fear of misfortune. Ibn Kathir also cites Ikrima, who said it concerned Abu Lubaba ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir, who gestured at the Banu Qurayza that they would be slaughtered, and al-Sudi, who mentions two men after Uhud who wished to seek protection with a Jew or a Christian. Al-Tabari judges the verse general and considers all these reports possible. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir distinguish between one who takes them as allies in belief, who becomes one of them in disbelief, and one who does so only in conduct, who incurs blame. Ibn 'Abbas derived from it the permission to eat the slaughter of Arab Christians. The following verses describe hypocrites who hasten toward these alliances fearing reversals of fortune, and who will be exposed when God grants victory or a command from Him; they will regret their duplicity, while the believers will marvel at their oaths and at their deeds, now void. Al-Tabari links the second verse to Ibn Ubayy, while others take it to refer to hypocrites in general.

This verse describes those with a sickness in their hearts, meaning hypocrisy and doubt, who hasten to befriend the Jews and Christians and excuse themselves by saying they fear misfortune may strike them and they will then need those allies. The commentators agree that these were Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions among the hypocrites. Ibn Abbas explained the fear as the possibility that the Prophet's affair would not succeed, while al-Kalbi and al-Sudi understood it as drought that would cut off the food and loans the hypocrites received from the Jews. God's reply, "perhaps Allah will bring victory," is taken as a certain promise because "perhaps" comes from God. The scholars differ on the victory: al-Sudi and others identify it as the conquest of Mecca, Qatada and Muqatil as a decisive judgment granting the Prophet victory over his opponents, and al-Dahhak as the conquest of Jewish settlements such as Khaybar and Fadak. As for "a command from Him," some mention the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir and the killing of the Banu Qurayza, others the jizya tax, the exposure of the hypocrites' secrets and an order to kill them, or the abundance granted to the Muslims. The hypocrites will then regret what they concealed within themselves, whether their doubt about the Prophet's mission or their alliance with the Jews. Several commentators add that the believers will then marvel at the hypocrites' emphatic oaths and that their deeds will be rendered void.

This verse describes the hypocrites when God exposes their true nature. The believers will marvel: are these the ones who swore by God with the strongest oaths that they were with them? Their deeds have failed, and they have become losers. The commentators agree that those with sickness in their hearts are the hypocrites, and that their alliance with Jews and Christians led to their exposure.

Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Wahidi understand these words as spoken by the believers when victory comes and the hypocrites are humiliated. Ibn 'Atiyya adds that the words may also recall what was said when the hypocrites feared reversals, and he notes the differing recitations. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report that believers may have addressed one another or the Jews themselves, since the hypocrites had sworn them support. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi stress the surprise and irony in the phrasing.

Most commentators take the words "their deeds have failed" to mean that deeds done without sincerity toward God earn no reward. On the occasion of revelation, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ishaq mention the Banu Qaynuqa and Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, while other reports differ, and the exegetes do not settle between them.

The commentators explain that God addresses the believers, warning that if any of them turns away from his religion, God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers and firm against the disbelievers, striving in God's cause without fearing the blame of any blamer. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi report that this promise was fulfilled through Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and his companions who fought the apostates after the Prophet's death, a view also transmitted from al-Hasan and Qatada. Al-Tabari, however, judges the view that these are the people of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, from Yemen, to be closer to the truth, relying on the hadith of 'Iyad al-Ash'ari narrated by Ahmad and al-Hakim. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and others mention both opinions without deciding between them. Al-Suddi says they are the Ansar, Mujahid says the people of Yemen, and others name the conquerors of Qadisiyya or the Persians, based on the hadith about Salman. The commentators read the attributes similarly: humility means tenderness and gentleness toward the believers rather than contempt, and might means firmness toward the disbelievers. On the love of God, al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari understand it as God's reward and pleasure and the servant's obedience, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin treat it as a real attribute. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi discuss the kinds of apostasy and the two readings of yartadd. All agree that the promise is a report of the unseen that attests to the truth of the Qur'an, and that the final grace is God's bounty, given to whom He wills.

This verse declares that the true guardianship of believers belongs to God, His Messenger, and the sincere believers who establish prayer, give zakat, and bow in humility before God. It follows the prohibition on taking Jews and Christians as allies and balances it by naming those whose friendship is required. The commentators agree that the word wali here means support, love, or protection; the particle innama signals exclusivity; and the singular form waliyyukum, though several are named, indicates that authority belongs to God in the primary sense and to the others only by derivation. According to al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, the phrase 'and those who believe' is general, and the attributes of prayer and zakat distinguish the sincere believer from the hypocrite.

Opinions differ on the phrase 'while bowing.' Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu al-Su'ud read it as humility and submission to God. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi take it as voluntary prayer or the bowing posture itself, linking it to the giving of zakat. Mujahid and al-Sudi report that the verse was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who gave his ring in charity while bowing in prayer; al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya regard these reports as weak, while al-Zamakhshari accepts the event as an example, noting that the plural form encourages others to imitate it.

The accounts of the occasion of revelation also vary. Ibn Ishaq and al-Wahidi mention 'Ubada ibn al-Samit, who renounced his alliance with the Banu Qaynuqa', while others recount 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, abandoned by their people. The commentators do not settle between these versions.

This part of the verse states that whoever takes Allah, His Messenger and the believers as allies belongs to the party of Allah, and that this party will prevail. Most commentators take hizb to mean soldiers or helpers: al-Hasan says they are the armies of Allah, Abu Ubayda and others say they are the supporters, and al-Tabari and al-Sudi identify them with the Ansar. Al-Tabari explains that victory means dominance over those who oppose and fight the believers. Al-Razi understands the word as companions who share one opinion, while al-Akhfash describes them as people who follow Allah's religion and obey Him. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan explain that the noun phrase stands in place of a pronoun, so the meaning is simply that they are the victors. This wording honours them and suggests that whoever allies with others belongs to the party of Satan. Al-Zamakhshari also considers that the party of Allah may refer to the Messenger and the believers. Ibn Kathir sees a promise of ultimate victory, even if believers may suffer temporary setbacks. Ibn 'Ashur connects the verse to the prohibition on taking Jews and Christians as allies, stressing that guardianship belongs to Allah and His Messenger. The commentators differ on the occasion of revelation of the preceding verses: most cite Ubada ibn al-Samit, who disavowed his alliance with the Jews, while others report different accounts.

This verse commands believers not to take as allies, helpers or friends those who have made their religion an object of mockery and play, whether among the People of the Book before them or among the disbelievers, and to fear God if they are truly believers. The commentators agree that the mockers are the Jews among the People of the Book and the polytheists among the disbelievers, and that the prohibition on alliance is grounded in this mockery: whoever behaves thus deserves enmity rather than friendship. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that this mockery meant professing Islam with the tongue while hiding disbelief in the heart, and al-Tabari compares it to the hypocrites of the Chapter of the Cow who told their devils that they were only mocking. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi hold that such mockery is answered not with alliance but with hatred and separation. The occasion of revelation, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerns Rifa'a ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Harith, who had feigned Islam before apostatising and whom some Muslims were befriending; others report that the mockery targeted the call to prayer and the worship of the Muslims. On the reading, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read the word for disbelievers in the genitive, linked to the People of the Book, while the others read it in the accusative, linked to the first relative pronoun; al-Tabari considers both readings correct and of the same meaning. Most exegetes take 'the disbelievers' here to mean specifically the polytheists, because of the gravity of their disbelief.

This verse describes how some disbelievers, among the People of the Book and the polytheists, mocked the call to prayer when it was made. When the believers were called to prayer, they took it as a jest and a game, laughing and mocking, and the Quran states that this stems from their lack of reason, since someone with sound intellect would not ridicule such an act of worship. The commentators relate, through al-Suddi and al-Tabari, the story of a Christian in Medina who, on hearing the muezzin proclaim that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, cursed the liar, and was then burned with his household when a spark from a lamp set his house on fire; Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy transmit it as well. Others report, through al-Kalbi and al-Baghawi, that the Jews would say of the Muslims who stood up to pray, 'They have stood up, may they not stand,' and would laugh at their bowing and prostration. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari take the verse as evidence that the adhan is established by the text of the Book and not by a dream alone, while Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi hold that it presupposes the adhan's legitimacy without itself establishing it. Commentators differ on whether the pronoun in 'ittakhadhuha' refers to the prayer or to the calling. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi observe that this is among the sharpest rebukes addressed to the learned, and the mockery of religion is a reason to refuse alliance with its mockers. Modern commentators such as al-Sha'rawi and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress the dignity of prayer and the value of the call to it.

This verse instructs the Prophet ﷺ to tell the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, that they have no real grievance against the believers except their faith in God, in what was revealed to them and in what was revealed before. Commentators read this as a rhetorical device that praises by seeming to blame. According to al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, it was revealed about Jews who, after hearing the Prophet mention Jesus, denied his prophethood. Al-Tabari explains that the verb naqama means to disapprove or to hold against, and notes that it has two vowel patterns, which al-Zajjaj and al-Nahhas also mention. The final clause, 'and that most of you are defiantly disobedient', divides the exegetes. Al-Tabari and most of the earlier commentators link it to 'that we believe', while al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan propose other readings, such as an implied cause, a meaning of 'together with', or an independent sentence. Ibn 'Atiyya considers the reading that links it to the believers' faith more coherent. Al-Razi observes that the word 'most' excludes the believers from the charge. Later passages, discussed by al-Wahidi, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, mention the curse, the transformation into apes and swine, and the worship of the taghut, which the commentators treat as a mocking answer to the claim that Islam is the worst religion. They agree that the purpose is to rebuke the disputants by recalling the misdeeds of their forebears.

This verse tells the Prophet to ask the People of the Book who mock the Muslims' religion whether he should inform them of something worse, in God's sight, than their resentment of the believers. The commentators explain the answer as those whom God cursed and with whom He became angry, some of whom He turned into apes and swine, and who worshipped the Taghut, namely the disobedient Jews. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan agree that the apes were the people of the Sabbath, while the swine were, for most, disbelievers from the table of Jesus. Ibn Abbas, in a report carried by Ibn Abi Talha, holds that both transformed groups were from the people of the Sabbath, the young turned into apes and the elders into swine. The readings differ on 'and worshipped the Taghut': the majority reads 'abada with the Taghut in the accusative, Hamza reads 'abud, an intensive form like hadhir, and others read plurals. Al-Farra' allows an implied relative pronoun. Most define the Taghut as anything worshipped besides God, though some identify it with Satan, the golden calf or soothsayers. Zamakhshari and Razi treat the worship of the Taghut as coordinated with the relative clause, and explain the verb 'made' as abandonment or divine decree, whereas al-Jubba'i reads it as creation. Ibn Kathir and al-Nasafi see the phrase 'worse in place' as a comparative used without a true point of comparison. Ibn Kathir also cites a hadith from Ibn Mas'ud that apes and swine left no descendants.

This verse describes a group of hypocrites among the Jews who came to the Prophet and the believers professing faith with their tongues while remaining in disbelief in their hearts. They entered with disbelief and left with it, unaffected by what they had heard. The commentators agree that the verse concerns the hypocrites. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Suddi say the pronoun refers to the Jews of the Prophet's time, especially the hypocrites among them. Al-Tabari explains that they showed confirmation with their tongues while concealing denial in their hearts. Al-Razi notes that the preposition bi indicates that disbelief stayed with them, without any reduction, both on entering and on leaving. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan observe that repeating the pronoun hum stresses the constancy of their state of disbelief, and that the particle qad conveys an expectation of the signs of hypocrisy becoming visible. Al-Zamakhshari reads the two clauses as circumstantial phrases meaning they entered disbelievers and left disbelievers. Ibn Zayd links the passage to a saying of some People of the Book mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran and holds that they returned to their disbelieving leaders. The closing words, God knows best what they conceal, are understood by several as referring to disbelief and hypocrisy, and Ibn Atiyya sees in them a way of exposing them. The scholars do not differ on the ruling but on the precise identity of the group and on the meaning of certain terms.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that he sees many of the Jews rushing towards sin, transgression and the consumption of unlawful gain, and He condemns this conduct. The commentators agree that sin refers to wrongdoing in general, transgression to injustice and encroachment on the rights of others, and soht to any unlawful earning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi note that the best-known form of soht is the bribe taken in judgment, while Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi add bribery in religious matters, and al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi also mention usury. Al-Suddi reads sin as disbelief, whereas Qatada limits the passage to Jewish judges and Ibn Zayd applies it to particular people among the Jews. Al-Tabari judges it preferable to take sin as all disobedience without excluding disbelief. The following phrase, which rebukes the rabbis and scholars for not forbidding them, is described by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak as the most severe verse in the Quran toward scholars. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that neglecting to forbid wrong is more blameworthy than committing it, since the word sun'a denotes a settled and mastered practice. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the rabbis and scholars meant are Jewish teachers, and that the verse includes silence in the face of wrongdoing. Taken together, the verse means that persistent corruption and the silence of the learned about it are both blameworthy.

This verse rebukes the Jewish scholars, the rabbis and the learned men, for failing to forbid their people from uttering falsehood and consuming what is unlawful. Al-Tabari explains that the rabbaniyyun were their leaders and governing scholars, and the ahbar their learned men and commanders. The sin of speech is understood as lies, since they wrote documents with their own hands and claimed they came from God, while the unlawful gain (suht) is the bribe taken for judging contrary to God's Book. Most commentators, from al-Wahidi and al-Razi to al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir, agree that "lawla" means "why did they not" and carries a strong reproach. Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak report that this is the most severe verse in the Quran toward scholars. Al-Hasan says the rabbaniyyun were scholars of the Gospel and the ahbar scholars of the Torah, whereas others hold that the whole passage concerns Jews. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud argue that the word "sana'a" (to craft) is stronger than "amila" (to do), since a craft implies mastery and training, so failing to forbid wrongdoing is worse than committing it. Ibn Ashur sees the change of verb as mere stylistic variety. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi note that the verse is a basis for the duty of enjoining good and forbidding evil, applying to scholars in particular.

The commentators explain that the verse reports the claim of the Jews that God's hand is chained, meaning that He is stingy and withholds His gifts. They said this when their provision was reduced after a time of plenty, and God replies that it is their own hands that are chained, that they are cursed for this saying, and that His two hands are outstretched, as He spends however He wills. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid take the chaining and outstretching of the hand as a figure for miserliness and generosity, al-Hasan reads it as the withholding of punishment, and al-Sudi as God holding back His hand until He returns their kingdom to them. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir affirm that God has two hands in a manner fitting to Him, while others read them as bounty, power or dominion; al-Zamakhshari treats the image as a metaphor for generosity, and Ibn Ashur explains the dual form as emphasis on abundance.

The commentators agree that the verse states that God cast enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection, that whenever they kindle the fire of war God extinguishes it, that they strive to spread corruption on earth, and that God does not love the corrupters. The next verse, according to Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari, promises the People of the Book forgiveness of their sins and Paradise if they believe and fear God, and abundance if they uphold the Torah and the Gospel, while distinguishing a moderate community from a majority who do evil.

The verse states that if the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, had believed in God and His Messenger Muhammad ﷺ and in what he brought, and had been mindful of God, God would have covered over their misdeeds without exposing them and would have admitted them to the Gardens of Bliss. The commentators broadly agree that faith and piety are the two conditions for expiation and entry into Paradise, but they differ on the meaning of piety. Al-Tabari and Qatada take it as avoiding what God has forbidden, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi as avoiding sins, including opposition to their own Scripture, while another view restricts it to avoiding associating partners with God. Al-Zamakhshari holds that faith alone does not save unless joined with piety, but Ibn al-Munir, in al-Insaf, replies that faith by itself erases what came before, as agreed by Sunnis and Mu'tazilites, and that piety understood as fear of God belongs to every believer. The verse goes on to promise that if they upheld the Torah, the Gospel and what was revealed to them, they would be given abundance. Ibn 'Abbas understood this as rain and plant growth, while al-Farra read it as a figure of speech for general prosperity. The verse then mentions a moderate community, which Ibn 'Abbas and al-Tabari identify with believers among the People of the Book such as Abdullah ibn Salam, while Mujahid and Ibn Zayd describe them as people faithful to God's obedience. As for the many, their wrongdoing consists chiefly in denying the prophets and distorting the Scriptures.

This verse says that if the People of the Book had truly upheld the Torah and the Gospel, and what was revealed to them from their Lord, meaning they applied their rulings and recognised in them the good news of the Prophet ﷺ and the Qur'an, they would have received blessings from every direction. Most commentators explain this literally: God would send rain from the sky and make the earth bring forth plants. Al-Farra' and others read it as a figure of speech for abundant provision, like the saying that someone is in ease from head to toe. Some take what was revealed to them to mean the Qur'an, others the books of the Israelite prophets, and Ibn 'Ashur holds that upholding these books requires acknowledging the Prophet. All agree that 'upholding' means acting on the books, not merely reciting them, and that piety is the condition for forgiveness of sins and entry into Paradise, as the previous verse states. The second part speaks of a moderate group among them. Most identify these as those who embraced Islam, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and the Negus. Al-Tabari reports that they were those who, concerning Jesus, affirmed he was God's servant and messenger, while Ibn Zayd and Qatada take them to be the people who obeyed God according to His Book. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi say they were a group that did not oppose the prophets as the rebels did. There is agreement that many of them did evil, and some name Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions. On the word sa'a, al-Zamakhshari treats it as meaning 'evil is', carrying a sense of wonder, while Ibn 'Atiyya takes it as an inflected verb meaning the deeds were bad.

This verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to convey everything revealed to him from his Lord, without fearing anyone or dreading harm. The commentators explain that concealing part of the message is like conveying none of it, since the message cannot be divided. They agree that the Prophet fully discharged his mission, and that God pledged to protect him from people, meaning from being killed or harmed in a way that would prevent him from conveying the message. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report Aisha's rebuttal of anyone claiming that the Prophet concealed part of the revelation, citing this verse. Several accounts of the occasion of revelation are given: the report from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi of a Bedouin who drew the Prophet's sword while he slept under a tree and whose hand trembled so the sword fell; the report that the Prophet had been guarded until this verse, after which he dismissed his guards; and Ibn Jurayj's report that the Prophet feared the Quraysh. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan prefer to read the verse as divine assurance against the plots of the People of the Book. Most commentators understand 'the people' to mean the disbelievers. On the closing phrase, al-Mawardi and others give two readings: God does not help the disbelievers reach their aims, or he does not guide them to Paradise.

God instructs His Prophet to tell the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, that they stand on nothing of real value until they uphold the Torah and the Gospel, meaning that they believe in them and act by them, together with what has been sent down to them from their Lord, which most commentators take to be the Qur'an. God then reports that many of them will increase in rebellion and disbelief through what is revealed to the Prophet, and He consoles him by telling him not to grieve over the disbelieving people. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi understand the required upholding as belief in the Prophet ﷺ and observance of the rulings not abrogated, while al-Zamakhshari explains that the word "thing" means a religion worthy of the name, so that they have no standing with God. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari hold that the increase in disbelief comes from rejecting the Qur'an, and Ibn Ashur attributes this hostility to envy and stubbornness. According to al-Tabari and al-Tha'alibi the consolation is a comfort to the Prophet rather than a prohibition on natural sorrow, a point al-Qurtubi also makes. Several commentators report, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, that the Jews told the Prophet they would keep only the Torah, an account recorded by al-Wahidi and Ibn al-Jawzi. Further differences concern the "moderate community" mentioned later in the chapter and the true nature of faith, which most link to belief in God, the Last Day and righteous deeds.

This verse states that the security from fear and grief promised on the Day of Judgment belongs to anyone who believes in God and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, whatever community they belong to: believers, Jews, Sabians or Christians. The criterion is faith and good action, not mere affiliation to a religion. Commentators differ on who is meant by "those who believed." Most, including Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn, take it to mean the Muslims. Al-Razi, following al-Zajjaj, and al-Sam'ani read it as the hypocrites who professed faith only with their tongues, while al-Qadi and al-Alusi include all who adhere to Muhammad's religion, sincere or hypocritical. The identity of the Sabians is also disputed: Mujahid places them between Christians and Magians, Sa'id ibn Jubayr between Jews and Christians, Qatada describes them as worshippers of angels, and others see them as a distinct group whose practices are described in several ways. The grammar is debated as well. Sibawayh, al-Khalil and the Basran grammarians hold that "al-sabi'un" is in the nominative as a topic with a deleted predicate and a delayed position, whereas al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' link it to the pronoun in "hadu" or to the place of "inna"; al-Zajjaj, al-Nahhas and al-Baydawi reject these readings. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the mention of the Sabians in this position signals that if they can be forgiven, others certainly can. Ibn 'Uthaymin stresses that faith alone is not enough without good works, and that belief in the Last Day includes everything the Prophet reported about what follows death.

This verse tells that God took a solemn covenant from the Children of Israel to believe in His oneness and follow His commands, and that He sent them messengers to teach them their religion. The commentators explain, however, that whenever a messenger came with what their souls did not desire, one group was called a liar and another group was killed. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi identify the rejected messengers as 'Isa and Muhammad and the slain as Zakariyya and Yahya, while Abu Hayyan and al-Nasafi hold that the denial was shared by Jews and Christians and that the killing was specific to the Jews. Al-Tabari and al-Mawardi explain that these acts broke the covenant and were boldness against God.

The commentators agree in describing the stubbornness of this people and their breach of the covenant, which they present as a recurring pattern across generations. Al-Zamakhshari, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi discuss the grammar of the conditional word "kullama": some assume an unstated response, others take "kadhdhabu" itself as the response. The present tense "yaqtulun" is, according to al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, used to make a past scene vivid and horrifying and to suit the verse endings. Al-Razi notes that placing the object first highlights the gravity of killing.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that following desire can lead to rejecting what reason does not accept, and Ibn 'Uthaymin compares this attitude to that of some theological schools.

The commentators explain that this verse describes the Children of Israel, with whom God had made a covenant and to whom He sent messengers. Whenever a messenger came with something their souls did not desire, they denied some and killed others, believing they would not be tested or punished for it. They became blind and deaf to the truth. God then forgave them, but many of them returned to blindness and deafness. God sees what they do and will repay them.

Most exegetes agree that blindness and deafness are a figure for straying from the truth, and that fitna means a trial or a punishment. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as a trial or chastisement, while al-Mawardi and Abu Hayyan distinguish between worldly and otherworldly forms of it. Al-Tabari reports from Ibn Abbas that it means idolatry, and Mujahid and Qatada link the verse to the Jews.

The meaning of God's forgiveness is disputed. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report that it was the lifting of the trial or their victory over enemies, and Ibn al-Jawzi also cites the sending of Muhammad ﷺ to call them to repentance. Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take it as the acceptance of their repentance, while al-Jalalayn states that they repented. Al-Wahidi and al-Sam'ani place this forgiveness after Moses, at the time of Jesus, or at the time of Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di treat the verse as a summary of successive episodes in their history, and al-Qasimi links it to the Babylonian and Roman destructions.

On the second blindness, al-Tabari links it to rejecting the truth, Ibn Kathir to disobedience, and al-Razi to their demand to see God and the wars that followed. Grammatically, most treat "kathir" as an apposition to the pronoun, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan discuss other constructions. The readings of "takun" with raised or lowered final vowel are discussed by Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi.

This verse states that those who say that God is the Messiah, son of Mary, have disbelieved, and that the Messiah himself told the Children of Israel to worship God, his Lord and theirs. Whoever associates partners with God, God forbids him Paradise, his refuge is the Fire, and the wrongdoers have no helpers. The commentators agree that those who said this were groups of Christians. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir link the statement to the Jacobites, while al-Baghawi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir also mention the Melkites and the Nestorians. They then rely on the fact that the Messiah acknowledged himself as a servant, that his mother was truthful, and that both ate food, which Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir read as a sign of need and createdness rather than divinity. Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the last clause may be the words of the Messiah or a statement by God confirming his words. Al-Razi concludes from it that the punishment of grave sinners is not eternal, a view answered by Ibn Juzayy and al-Biqa'i, who limit the threat to disbelief. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Qurtubi note that the particle inna with the pronoun gives emphasis and causal sense. On the exact meaning of the Trinity formula, Abu Hayyan, al-Razi and Ibn Kathir describe the various Christian explanations, and several commentators take it to mean three gods: God, Jesus and Mary. Opinions thus differ on the details, while the general condemnation of associating partners with God is accepted by all.

This verse states that those who say that God is the third of three have disbelieved, that there is only one God, and that those who do not stop saying this will suffer a painful punishment. The commentators generally agree that the verse condemns the Christian groups who professed the Trinity, though they differ on how this doctrine was formulated. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that, according to these Christians, God is one substance with three hypostases: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi also give the interpretation that the three are God, Jesus and his mother Mary, pointing to the verse asking Jesus whether he told people to take him and his mother as two gods besides God. Al-Razi calls the doctrine plainly contrary to reason and considers it among the most corrupt ideas in the world. Ibn 'Atiyya notes that the Christian sects, including the Melkites and Nestorians, held differing positions. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the word 'min' in 'among them' may mark a specification, identifying the disbelievers as Christians, or a partition, meaning only those who persisted, since many of them repented. Abu Hayyan and Ibn Kathir observe that the punishment applies in this world and in the hereafter. The next verse invites repentance and seeking forgiveness, and Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di stress God's forgiveness and mercy toward those who return to Him. Ibn Kathir rejects the view attributed to Abu Sakhr that the verse also refers to Jews. Al-Zamakhshari and others read the mention of Jesus and Mary's humanity, shown by their eating food, as proof that they are not divine.

This verse calls on the Christians who claim that the Messiah is divine or who hold the doctrine of the Trinity to repent and seek forgiveness, after God has declared their disbelief and warned them. It also states that God is oft-forgiving and merciful toward those who return to Him. The commentators agree that the interrogative form expresses rebuke and astonishment at their persistence in disbelief, and that the aim is to urge them to abandon the belief in the Trinity and in the divinity of Jesus, and to ask forgiveness for the past. Al-Farra' and those who follow him hold that the question carries the force of a command, as in the verse 'Will you not desist?'. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di see in it a sign of God's generosity, kindness and mercy, since He calls them to repentance despite the gravity of their sin and accepts whoever turns back. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud link the verse to what precedes it: repentance means giving up the false belief and returning to monotheism, while seeking forgiveness means asking pardon for what has passed. Ibn 'Ashur explains that the verse combines warning and encouragement, and that the present tense in 'what they say' indicates continuity. Ibn 'Uthaymin discussed the conditions of repentance and noted a disagreement over whether repentance from one sin is valid while persisting in another. All the commentators close with the names 'the Oft-Forgiving' and 'the Most Merciful', which encourage hope that repentance will be accepted.

This verse states that the Messiah, son of Mary, was a messenger like those who came before him, not a god or the son of God, and that his mother was a woman of great truthfulness, who affirmed the signs and words of God. The commentators agree that it refutes the Christian groups who declared the Messiah to be God or one of three. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and al-Nasafi argue that his miracles do not make him divine, since similar wonders occurred through Moses, whose staff became a serpent, and the creation of Adam without father or mother is even more remarkable. On the mention of eating food, most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari, take it literally as proof of need and dependence, which cannot belong to a god. Al-Mawardi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Qutayba and Ibn al-Jawzi report another view, that it alludes to the bodily functions that follow eating; Ibn 'Atiyya finds this crude and unnecessary, while al-Baydawi and Ibn Juzayy hold that the argument stands either way. On Mary's title of sincerity, opinions differ: some see moral uprightness, others faith in God's words and in her son. Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi conclude from this description that she was not a prophetess, whereas al-Qurtubi considers that inference debatable. The closing phrase, 'see how they are turned away', is read by the commentators as wonder at people who turn away despite clear proof, the word 'then' marking the gap between the two surprises, according to al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ to rebuke those who worship other than God, namely the Christians who worship Jesus, by asking how they can worship one who holds no power to harm or benefit them, while God alone hears and knows. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Atiyya, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Shawkani take the reference to be Jesus and his mother, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi explain that Jesus has such power only through God's grant and not by his own essence, and that whatever harm or benefit humans can bring comes by God's empowerment. Al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi mention harm before benefit because guarding against harm is more important. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan read the divine attributes as a reminder of human limitation, whereas Ibn Kathir sees the mention of hearing and knowledge as a warning to the idolater. Al-Razi offers several rational arguments against Jesus's divinity, such as his need for food and his inability to defend himself. Commentators differ on whether (ma) refers to a thing or to a category, as Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur note, and on the extent of the incapacity ascribed to the Messiah. Ibn Kathir and al-Shawkani also relate the circumstances of revelation concerning the Christians, yet the verse itself centres on the affirmation of God's oneness and the rejection of divinity for a creature.

God commands His Prophet to address the People of the Book, whom most commentators take to mean Jews and Christians together, and to forbid them from exaggeration in their religion, meaning going beyond due limits either in excess or in neglect. The commentators agree that the blamed exaggeration is the false kind: the Jews went too far against Jesus by calling his birth illegitimate, and the Christians exalted him to divinity. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi understand the address to include both groups, while Ibn 'Atiyya holds that it is mainly directed at Christians, with the prohibition on following the passions of the Jews meaning not to imitate their error. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan distinguish a true exaggeration, which is deep investigation of evidence as practised by the rational theologians, from a false one, which is ignoring proofs and following doubts. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi report that the 'passions' concern the earlier ancestors and leaders who went astray before the Prophet's mission and led many others astray, and then went further astray by rejecting him. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim explain the repetition of the verb 'went astray' as three degrees of error, and al-Razi notes that the word hawa is always used in a negative sense. Regarding 'the right path' (sawa' al-sabil), most commentators see it as the straight and balanced way, lying between excess and neglect.

This verse states that unbelievers among the Children of Israel were cursed through the tongues of David and Jesus son of Mary, that is, in the Psalms and the Gospel, because of their disobedience and transgression. The commentators differ on the meaning of the curse. Al-Tabari, relying on Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Kathir hold that they were cursed in every revealed book, the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel and the Quran. Mujahid, Qatada and Abu Malik understand it as a transformation, some turned into apes under David and others into swine under Jesus. Al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and al-Tha'alabi recount the story of the people of Ayla who broke the Sabbath and became apes, and of the disbelievers among the table-companions, against whom Jesus prayed and who became swine. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Asamm argue that David and Jesus foretold Muhammad and cursed those who would reject him. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya explain that the curse means distance from God's mercy and that the transformation is not what the wording suggests. On the sin itself, most commentators explain that they did not forbid one another from evil. Ibn Kathir, Ibn Ashur and al-Baydawi cite the hadith transmitted by Ibn Mas'ud, in which people who sat and ate with sinners after rebuking them were condemned. The following verses, read by al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan as continuing this theme, condemn those who side with unbelievers, whom Ibn Kathir identifies as hypocrites and al-Jaza'iri and the Jalalayn as the Jews of Medina.

This verse explains that the Children of Israel did not forbid one another from the wrongs they committed, and that this neglect is the reason for the blame and the divine astonishment at their conduct, emphasized by an oath. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Nasafi take the phrase to mean that they did not forbid one another from repeating a wrong or from committing a similar one. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that this failure to forbid is itself a disobedience and a transgression, and that the blame is directed at this neglect.

The commentators agree that a blameworthy act is anything the sacred law prohibits, though most do not specify which acts are meant. Ibn al-Jawzi lists several examples: hunting fish on the Sabbath, taking bribes in judgment, and consuming usury. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi relate the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud that the decline of the Children of Israel began when they sat with wrongdoers without rebuking them, and the Prophet's saying that one must enjoin good and forbid evil. From this they derive the duty to forbid wrongdoing.

The scholars differ on who is meant by those who take the disbelievers as allies. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid identify them as the hypocrites, while al-Baghawi and al-Razi relate that the reference is to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, who helped the polytheists of Mecca against the Prophet. Al-Razi notes that the seeing may be with the heart or the eye, and Ibn Juzayy considers the eye-sight to be the more apparent meaning for the Prophet's contemporaries. Ibn 'Ashur and Abu Hayyan differ on whether this sentence is an independent statement.

This verse describes how many of the Children of Israel, already cursed through David and Jesus, aligned themselves with the disbelievers, taking them as allies, supporting them and cooperating with them. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, understand this to refer to the Jews, and cite Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions who went to the Meccan polytheists to incite them against the Prophet. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan, as reported by al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan, hold that the reference is to the hypocrites among the People of the Book who sided with the Jews or the polytheists. The phrase about what their souls had sent ahead is explained by most as their deeds for the Hereafter: this alliance brought God's wrath upon them and an eternal stay in punishment. Grammarians and exegetes differ on how to parse 'that God was angry with them': al-Zamakhshari and al-Zajjaj treat it as a specifying complement or an apposition, while Abu Hayyan finds some of these readings incorrect according to Sibawayh. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya report traditions about the duty to enjoin good and forbid evil, whose neglect is cited as the sin of the Israelites. Ibn Ashur argues that many Jews of Medina who outwardly professed Islam out of hypocrisy are meant. Ibn Uthaymin distinguishes degrees of alliance with disbelievers and takes divine anger in its apparent sense. The commentaries agree that alliance with unbelievers is forbidden and that it is the cause of their loss.

This verse states that sincere faith in God, His Prophet and what was revealed to him would prevent a believer from taking unbelievers as allies, and that such an alliance shows a flaw in faith. Most commentators understand the preceding verses as addressing the People of the Book from the Children of Israel, while Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan take the subject to be the hypocrites who allied with the Jews or polytheists. Al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi identify the "disbelievers" with the polytheists of Mecca, whereas Ibn 'Ashur holds that they were Jews of Medina who had outwardly embraced Islam out of hypocrisy.

The commentators agree that fisq here means departure from obedience to God, but differ on its gravity. Al-Tabari and al-Sam'ani describe it as disobedience and making lawful what God forbade, while Ibn Kathir speaks of departing from obedience to God and His messenger. Ibn 'Uthaymin reads it as the major fisq that takes a person out of the religion. Al-Qurtubi infers from the verse that whoever takes an unbeliever as an ally and approves his deeds is not a believer. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi understand it as persistence in disbelief and hypocrisy.

The condition in the verse is also read in two ways. Al-Razi, al-Tabari and al-Qasimi take it to mean that had the Jews truly believed in Moses and the Torah they would not have allied with the polytheists, while Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi understand it as sincere faith in Muhammad and the Qur'an. Ibn Juzayy and al-Biqa'i link the verse to the surrounding passages on failing to forbid wrongdoing, a theme Ibn Kathir supports with many hadiths.

This verse states that the Jews and the polytheists are the fiercest enemies of the believers, while the Christians are the closest to them in affection. The commentators note that these qualities describe groups in general, not every individual. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the verse concerns the delegation sent by the Negus of Abyssinia, who wept and embraced Islam on hearing the Quran. Mujahid identifies them as the envoys who came with Ja'far from Abyssinia, while Qatada says they were people who kept to the law of Jesus and believed in Muhammad when he came. Al-Tabari judges that the verse describes a certain group without naming them, and that it may refer to the Negus's companions or to people following Jesus's law. As for the reason for this closeness, most exegetes point to the presence among them of priests and monks, that is scholars and worshippers, and to their lack of arrogance before the truth. Al-Razi adds that the Jews are more greedy for worldly gain while the Christians are less so. Al-Jassas and Abu Hayyan warn against reading the verse as praise of all Christians, though Abu Hayyan judges that Christians are generally in a better state than Jews. Ibn 'Ashur notes that priests and monks were known among the Arabs for their good character. Accounts of the occasion of revelation cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi are debated for their soundness.

This verse describes two groups, the Jews and the polytheists, and the Christians, in their attitude toward the believers. According to the commentators, the Jews and the polytheists are the most hostile to the believers, while those who say "we are Christians" are the closest to them in affection. They explain this closeness by the presence among them of learned priests, qissisin, and monks, ruhban, and by their freedom from arrogance before the truth. The verse then describes those who, on hearing the Qur'an, see their eyes overflow with tears for what they have recognized as true, and say: "Our Lord, we believe, so write us down among the witnesses." Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most commentators report that this refers to the Negus and his companions, or to the Abyssinian delegation that came to the Prophet, although the accounts differ on their number and on the date of revelation. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Kathir understand the "witnesses" to be the community of Muhammad, who will bear witness over the other peoples on the Day of Resurrection; al-Hasan takes them to be those who bear witness to faith, and others such as al-Zajjaj and al-Jubba'i mention the prophets and the believers. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that the passage concerns a category of people rather than all Christians, and several commentators note that tears may have flowed from some who did not believe. The reward promised is gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will abide forever, the recompense of the good-doers; as for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.

The commentators explain that this verse records the words of some People of the Book who believed upon hearing the Qur'an. Expressing their faith, they say: what prevents us from believing in God and in the truth that has come to us, when we hope that our Lord will admit us among the righteous people? Most agree that "the righteous people" are the obedient believers, and most often the community of Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Tabari understands them as believers who deserve Paradise through their obedience, while Ibn Zayd identifies them as the Prophet and his companions; Ibn al-Jawzi reports other views from Ibn Abbas and Muqatil, naming the companions or the first emigrants. On the word "hope", Ibn Kathir and others take it as a longing rather than a certainty, and Ibn Uthaymin notes that one should not testify to one's own entry into Paradise. Regarding the occasion of revelation, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi relate that the verses concern the delegation of al-Najashi, who wept on hearing the Qur'an and embraced Islam; Ibn Kathir considers this view problematic since the surah came after the episode of Ja'far, and al-Tabari keeps a broader application. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi read "What is the matter with us?" as a rhetorical question of disapproval at the absence of faith when its motive is present; others see it as a reply to those who reproached them, or as an inner voice dispelling doubts. Grammarians debate whether the "wa" before "we hope" marks a circumstantial clause or a coordination, without changing the essential meaning. The commentators conclude that the reward mentioned next follows from faith joined with knowledge and sincerity.

This verse tells us that God rewarded those who said, "Our Lord, we believe, so write us among the witnesses," and who hoped to enter Paradise with the righteous, with gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they will remain forever; this is the reward of the good-doers, that is, the sincere monotheists. The commentators agree that these verses were revealed about the Negus and his Christian companions, who wept and believed on hearing the Qur'an, though they differ on the number of those involved and on the details of the account. Ibn 'Abbas reports that Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recited Surah Maryam to them, while Sa'id ibn Jubayr mentions the delegation of seventy men to whom the Prophet recited Surah Ya-Sin. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi explain that good-doing includes pure monotheism, belief in the prophets, performing the obligations and avoiding sins. Al-Baghawi holds that the reward is attached to the speech because it accompanies sincerity and knowledge, while al-Nasafi holds that affirmation belongs to faith and rebuts the Karramiyya, who make faith mere utterance. Al-Razi concludes from the verse that a believer who commits a grave sin does not remain forever in Hell. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi differ on the force of the preposition in "what they recognised of the truth" and on certain grammatical functions. Some commentaries also discuss the occasion of revelation of the following verses, concerning companions who wished to renounce worldly pleasures, and the meaning of "gardens" and "rivers".

This verse states the fate of those who disbelieve and deny Our signs: they are the companions of the Blazing Fire, meaning they remain in it and never leave. The commentators explain that disbelief here means rejecting the oneness of God and denying the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, while denial refers to rejecting the verses of the Book. Al-Tabari notes that al-Jahim is the fire whose heat is most intense. Most exegetes, including al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy, set this verse against the reward of the believers who said, Our Lord, we believe, and were given gardens watered by rivers, so that promise and warning stand side by side. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi see in the linking of denial to disbelief a way of describing the deniers in contrast with the believers, pairing reward with threat. Ibn 'Ashur reads it as a safeguard, so that no listener imagines the reward covers all People of the Book. According to Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, the preceding verses were revealed about the Negus and his companions, or a Christian delegation that embraced Islam after hearing the Quran. Al-Razi draws from this verse that a believer who commits grave sins does not remain in the Fire forever, a conclusion the other commentators cited here do not share.

This verse forbids believers from making unlawful the good things God has made lawful for them, and from transgressing the limits. The commentators explain that the "good things" are the lawful pleasures of food, drink and marriage, and that transgression means going beyond what God has prescribed by turning to the forbidden, or by excess in the permitted. Most exegetes link its revelation to a group of Companions, among them Uthman ibn Maz'un, Ali and Ibn Mas'ud, who wished to renounce women, pleasant food and sleep. The Prophet replied that he fasts and breaks his fast, prays and sleeps, and marries, and that whoever turns away from his sunna is not of him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report several versions of this occasion, and Ibn Kathir notes that they support one another despite some broken chains of transmission.

The commentators agree that Islam rejects excessive asceticism and the personal prohibition of what is lawful, and that the verse addresses anyone who makes lawful for himself what God has made lawful, whether by belief, by words or by abstention. They differ on the meaning of "do not transgress": al-Sudi and Ikrima take it as an emphasis on the previous prohibition; al-Hasan takes it as a ban on declaring the forbidden lawful after forbidding the lawful; Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada understand it as a reference to castration. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur read it as a warning against moving from the lawful to the unlawful or against excess in the permitted.

On the person who declares a lawful thing forbidden to himself, jurists differ, as al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report: Malik and al-Shafi'i hold that it does not become forbidden and that no expiation is due, while Ahmad and Abu Hanifa require an oath expiation, with the wife excepted according to some. The verse also reminds that faith entails piety, and calls people to eat the lawful and good provision God grants.

This verse tells believers to eat of the provision God has given them, provided it is lawful and good, and to be mindful of God, in whom they believe. The commentators broadly agree on the core meaning: the verse forbids depriving oneself of permitted good things. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that the word provision here refers to food that is permitted, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya hold that the verb to eat covers enjoyment of food, drink, clothing and riding, with food singled out because it is the most important. Al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the verse was revealed concerning companions of the Prophet who wanted to give up worldly pleasures, some vowing to abstain from meat, sleep or women, and that the Prophet corrected them by describing his own way of life. Al-Razi notes that the particle min implies partiality and so warns against excess. Abu Hayyan lists several forms of forbidding, by statement, by action or by oath, and Ibn 'Ashur sees a general rule against prohibiting what God has not prohibited. On whether one who forbids a permitted thing must make expiation, al-Shawkani reports that most scholars say no, while Abu Hanifa and Ahmad require expiation, and Ibn Kathir presents both positions. Modern commentaries such as Ibn 'Uthaymin stress that true faith entails piety, and that good things are praiseworthy as long as they do not lead to arrogance or excess.

This verse teaches that God does not hold believers to account for the idle oath, the words that slip from the tongue without intention, but holds them responsible for what their hearts have truly bound themselves to. According to Ibn 'Abbas and others, it was revealed concerning companions who had forbidden themselves certain good things by oath; when told not to do so, they asked how to treat their oaths, and the expiation was then prescribed. Al-Shafi'i and most exegetes understand the idle oath as saying 'no, by God' or 'yes, by God' without intent, while Malik and others see it as swearing to something one believes true but which proves otherwise. The expiation is feeding ten needy people from the middling food with which one feeds one's family, clothing them, or freeing a slave; failing these, fasting three days. Scholars agree on the choice among the first three, but differ on the amount of food: al-Shafi'i, Ibn 'Abbas and Zayd ibn Thabit say one mudd per person, 'Umar, 'Ali and Abu Hanifa half a sa' of wheat, while 'Ali and Muhammad ibn Ka'b speak of a midday and evening meal, and some suggest judging by the means of the one who pays. On clothing, Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid speak of one garment, al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin of two, and Malik of what suffices for prayer. Al-Shafi'i requires the freed slave to be a believer, by analogy with the expiation for manslaughter, which Abu Hanifa does not accept. Most do not consider consecutive days obligatory for the fast, although the reading attributed to Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy makes it so. The verse closes by urging care with oaths, not multiplying them nor breaking them without cause, and by noting that God thus makes His signs clear so that you may be grateful.

This verse forbids believers wine, gambling, stone altars and divining arrows, calling them an abomination from Satan's handiwork, and orders them to avoid these things so that they may prosper. The commentators agree on the meanings: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi understand khamr as anything that clouds the mind, maysir as gambling in all its forms, ansab as idols or stones set up for sacrifice, and azlam as the arrows used to seek a decision. According to al-Mawardi and Ibn 'Atiyya, the verse came after a dispute among the Companions, and the prohibition came gradually, with the final ban after Uhud. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report the majority view that wine is najis in itself, while Rabi'a, al-Layth and al-Muzani hold it pure and forbid only drinking it. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy state that every intoxicant is wine and that small amounts are forbidden like large ones. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur allow certain contests, such as horse racing and archery, while others restrict wagering more tightly. The interrogative form, 'Will you then desist?', is considered stronger than a direct command, and 'Umar said: we have desisted. The following verses state that those who drank before the prohibition bear no blame if they feared God, believed and did good.

This verse states that Satan wants, through wine and gambling, to sow enmity and hatred among the believers and to turn them away from the remembrance of God and from prayer, and it closes with a question that urges them to stop. Commentators define khamr as any intoxicant and maysir as gambling; most identify the ansab with idols or stones on which sacrifices were made, and the azlam with divining arrows. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the prohibition of wine came in stages over several verses, and that when this verse was revealed Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'We have stopped, we have stopped.' The accounts of the occasion of revelation differ: Umar's prayer for a clear ruling, the quarrel between Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and an Ansari man, or a fight between two Ansar tribes; al-Tabari holds that the ruling binds everyone whatever the cause. Al-Razi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari explain that the enmity from wine arises because the drunkard does things that provoke quarrels, and the enmity from gambling arises because the loser who has lost his wealth resents the winner. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir take rijs as impure or repugnant; al-Qurtubi reports that most scholars see it as ritual impurity, while Rabi'a, al-Layth and al-Muzani hold wine to be pure. Ibn 'Ashur stresses that the rijs here is chiefly moral. The commentators agree on the firmness of the prohibition and on reading the question 'Will you then desist?' as a command.

In this verse God commands the believers to obey Him and His Messenger and to beware of disobedience, after having forbidden them wine, gambling, sacrificial stones and divining arrows. The commentators explain that obeying God and the Messenger includes avoiding all that is forbidden and performing what is obligatory, while beware means guarding against disobedience and its consequences. The phrase "if you turn away" refers to refusal and rebellion. As for "know that the duty of Our Messenger is only to convey clearly", it means that the Messenger has fulfilled his task of clear transmission, so the refusal of others does not harm him but harms those who turn away. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi read it as a warning to those who disobey, whereas Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn Sa'di stress that the Messenger was charged only with conveying the message, and that guidance and harm return to the addressees themselves.

Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi draw from the passage the prohibition of intoxicants and hold that every intoxicating drink is forbidden, while some scholars such as Rabi'a, al-Layth and al-Muzani debated the ritual purity of wine. The commentators report that the prohibition came gradually, and most place the revelation of this verse after the battle of Uhud.

This verse addresses the status of what believers consumed, namely wine and gambling, before these were forbidden. Some companions feared that those of their brothers who had died while drinking had incurred sin. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, the verse removes blame from those who drank before the prohibition, provided they were pious, faithful and did righteous deeds. Tabari and Ibn Kathir note that most reports on the occasion of revelation concern martyrs of Uhud who drank wine before its prohibition, and that some traditions attribute to Ibn Abbas and Umar a reading of the verse applied to those who drink after the ban.

The commentators agree on the general sense: God lifts blame from those who ate or drank lawful things, provided they avoid what is forbidden. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya explain that the phrase covers all lawful food and drink, whereas Tabari understands it as concerning the period before the prohibition. All accept the repetition of piety and faith as marking a progression, and they agree that God loves the doers of good.

Opinions differ on the three stages. Most say they refer to the act of fearing God. Al-Razi reports several readings, including that of Abu Bakr al-Asamm, who sees a chronology: before, during and after the prohibition. Tabari sees acceptance of God's command, then steadfastness, and finally goodness through voluntary acts. Ibn Juzayy and Abu Hayyan also report that some take the stages as avoiding polytheism, then major sins, then minor ones. Al-Zamakhshari stresses kindness towards others. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya also relate accounts of Qudama ibn Mazun, whose reading of the verse was rejected by Umar.
