This verse announces that God will test the believers with land game that comes near them while they are in ihram, so close that their hands and spears can reach it, in order to show who fears Him although unseen and who transgresses after this warning, for whom there is a painful punishment. The commentators agree that it was revealed in the year of Hudaybiyya, when wild animals and birds surrounded the companions who were in the sacred state, and that the test concerns land game rather than sea game. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Abbas explain that what the hands can reach refers to the young and the eggs, and what the spears can reach refers to large animals, while Ibn Atiyya sees the mention of hands and spears as pointing to the different means of hunting. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi argue that the word 'some' lessens the severity of the trial, whereas Ibn Ashur holds that the indefiniteness signals variety rather than insignificance. On the meaning of 'that God may know', many take it to mean that what is known becomes manifest, and al-Razi and al-Nasafi understand it as the fear actually existing in the one who fears. 'In secret' means either not seeing God or being alone away from people's eyes. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Uthaymin relate that the painful punishment may be in the hereafter, while Ibn Abbas reports beating and stripping of clothes. The jurists cited agree that hunting is forbidden in the state of ihram, though they differ on sea game, on hunting by a non-pilgrim inside the sanctuary, and on eating what a pilgrim has hunted.

The verse forbids believers from killing land game while they are in ihram for pilgrimage or umrah, or while they are within the sacred precinct. Whoever kills it deliberately, knowing the prohibition, must offer a compensation like what he killed from the livestock, judged by two just men among the Muslims. It is brought as an offering reaching the Ka'ba and given to the poor of the sacred precinct, or its value is spent on food for the needy, or he fasts the equivalent, so that he may taste the consequence of his deed. The commentators agree that this is both a penalty and an expiation. What happened before the prohibition is pardoned by God, and whoever returns to it will face God's retribution.

Scholars differ on what counts as deliberate. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and al-Zuhri take it to mean killing while knowing one is in ihram. Mujahid, Ibrahim and Ibn Jurayj take it to mean aiming at the game while having forgotten the state of ihram. Dawud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr hold that only deliberate killing incurs compensation, whereas the majority, including Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa, hold that error and forgetfulness also carry it. Those who impose a compensation on the repeat offender understand the retribution as punishment in the hereafter as well as expiation, while Ibn 'Abbas and Shurayh say no compensation is due after the first time.

On the meaning of equivalence, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad and most scholars consider physical resemblance, so a camel for the ostrich, a cow for the wild ass and a sheep for the gazelle, as the Companions ruled, and al-Shafi'i takes a sheep for the dove. Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf consider monetary value, while al-Nakha'i has the animal valued and a livestock offering bought with the sum. Scholars also differ on where the food or fast must be done: al-Shafi'i and 'Ata' require the sacred precinct, Malik the place of the offence, and Abu Hanifa leaves it open.

This verse states that the game of the sea and its food are lawful for the believers, whether they are in the state of ihram or not, and that they are a provision for the resident and the traveller alike. The commentators agree that the game of the sea means what is taken alive from its waters, and that the sea includes rivers, springs and pools. They differ over the meaning of its food. Abu Bakr, Umar, Ibn Umar, Abu Ayyub and Qatada, and Ibn Abbas in one report, understood it as what the sea casts up dead on the shore, citing the saying that its water is pure and its dead creatures lawful. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Nakha'i and al-Suddi took it to mean salted fish. Al-Tabari preferred the first view, since salted fish already falls under the game. Others took it to mean the salt that forms from the water, or what the water causes to grow. As for land game, it is forbidden to the pilgrim in ihram. The scholars differ on game hunted by someone not in ihram and offered to the pilgrim. Ali, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Umar forbade it entirely. Umar, Uthman in one report, Abu Hurayra, Ata', Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr allowed it if it was not hunted for him. Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad forbade what was hunted for him and allowed the rest. The verse ends with a call to fear God and a reminder that all will be gathered before Him.

The commentators explain that God made the Kaaba, the Sacred House, a support (qiyam) for people, meaning a foundation for both their religion and their worldly life, since they make pilgrimage to it and find safety within its sanctuary. The sacred months, the offerings and the garlands serve the same purpose. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi report that the Kaaba was named for its square shape or its height, and that it is called sacred because God forbade hunting there, cutting its trees and uprooting its grass. Most agree that "the people" here refers to the Arabs of the pre-Islamic era, and that the sacred months are Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja, al-Muharram and Rajab. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi understand this support as security, trade and the gathering of people. Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the garlands could be those adorning the offerings or those worn by pilgrims, taken from the trees of the sanctuary. Ibn Ashur takes "the sacred month" as a generic term rather than one particular month. For al-Razi, the purpose of all this is that people should know that God knows what is in the heavens and on earth, while al-Tabari reads it as God's knowledge of human welfare. Ibn Amir's reading qiyaman without the alif is also noted.

This verse states that God is severe in punishment toward those who violate His sanctities and persist in disobedience, and that He is Forgiving and Merciful toward those who keep His limits and repent. Al-Tabari explains that God knows what is hidden and what is apparent in people's deeds and counts them in order to repay them: His punishment is severe for whoever disobeys Him, while His forgiveness and mercy belong to whoever obeys Him and turns back to Him. Most commentators read the verse as the conclusion of the rulings that precede it on the state of consecration (ihram), hunting on land and at sea, the Ka'ba, the sacred month, the offerings and the garlands: it is a warning to those who treat these sanctities lightly and a promise to those who protect them. Al-Razi notes that faith is complete only through both hope and fear, and that the verse ends on mercy, which suggests that mercy prevails. Ibn 'Ashur sees it as a summary of the ways God deals with people: He punishes those who break His commands and forgives those who repent and do good.

There is broad agreement on the overall meaning. Ibn Sa'di says these two truths must be held firmly in the heart, so that they produce fear of punishment and hope for forgiveness. Ibn 'Uthaymin adds that combining the two names means forgiveness answers sin and mercy answers obedience, and he warns against reading the verse as making disobedience seem trivial.

The main difference concerns why the verse places the two parts in this order: some hold that fear should come before hope, while others hold that mercy deserves to close the verse. This disagreement does not change the general meaning of the verse.

This verse states that the Messenger's duty is only to convey the message, and that God knows what people show and what they conceal. Al-Tabari reads it as a warning: the Messenger delivers God's message, warns of punishment and promises reward, while God knows who obeys and who refuses, including what hearts hide of faith, disbelief or hypocrisy. Commentators broadly agree that the Prophet has done what was required of him, so the responsibility now rests with people and they have no excuse for neglect, as al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi stress. Al-Razi links the verse to what precedes it, the call to fear and to hope: the Messenger is charged only with conveying, and the rest belongs to God, who is severe in punishment and forgiving toward those who obey. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that it is not a verse of truce abrogated by the verses of fighting, but a description of the situation of one who has professed faith, since the Messenger then has no further task than conveying. Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan report the disagreement between those who consider it firm and those who consider it abrogated by the verse of the sword. Al-Qurtubi notes that the Messenger holds neither guidance, success nor reward, a point he presents as a rebuttal of the Qadariyya. Ibn 'Ashur and Ibn 'Uthaymin explain that the restriction is relative, since the Prophet has other duties, and that guidance belongs to God. Al-Sa'di concludes that the Prophet delivered as he was commanded and that the reckoning is God's alone.

The commentators explain that this verse commands the Prophet ﷺ to tell people that the bad and the good are not equal, even if the abundance of the bad impresses them. They differ on the meaning of the terms. Al-Hasan and Ibn Abbas, followed by al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi, understand them as the unlawful and the lawful; al-Suddi understands them as the disbeliever and the believer; others take them as the poor and the good, or the disobedient and the obedient. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan hold that the wording is general, covering wealth, deeds, people and knowledge: the bad does not thrive even when numerous, while the good, even when small, has a fine outcome. Al-Razi separates bodily impurity from spiritual impurity, the worst of which is ignorance and disobedience. Al-Baydawi, Abu al-Su'ud and Ibn Kathir stress that quality, not quantity, is the measure, so a little lawful gain is better than much unlawful gain. Al-Tabari explains that the people of understanding are those who grasp God's signs, and that success (falah) means attaining what is with God. Several reports say the verse was revealed about the pilgrims of Yamama, whom the Muslims wished to attack, though other accounts are also given. The verse thus warns against being dazzled by numbers.

In this verse God addresses the believers and tells them not to ask too much about matters they have not been commanded to, since disclosing them could grieve them and become a burden, while questions asked during the descent of the Quran are answered and therefore permitted. The commentators report that the occasion of revelation was the repeated questioning of the Prophet until he grew angry, including Abdullah ibn Hudhafa's question about his father, and the question whether pilgrimage was due every year, transmitted through Ibn Abbas, Anas, Abu Hurayra and Ali. Al-Tabari, whose view is widely followed, gathers these reports without favouring one. Ibn Abbas, in one transmission, links the verse to the bahira, sa'iba, wasila and ham, a view supported by Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, whereas Ikrima relates it to requests for miraculous signs. Most read the phrase 'God has pardoned it' as God's silence on such matters, so that what the law leaves unmentioned is a mercy, as cited by Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi, while others take it as pardon for what was already asked. Al-Razi, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that asking about matters whose disclosure would bring a heavy obligation or disgrace is forbidden, whereas asking about what the Quran expounds is allowed. Al-Qurtubi notes that some scholars, including Malik, Umar and Zayd ibn Thabit, disliked the multiplication of hypothetical legal questions, though not all extended this to questions about real events. As for 'A people before you asked such things and then became disbelievers', most take it to mean earlier nations such as the people of Salih or the followers of Jesus, who demanded signs or commandments and then rejected faith once these were granted.

This verse warns the believers against pressing with questions about matters that have not been explained to them. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that earlier peoples asked their prophets for specific signs or things, and after they were granted, they denied what they had received: the people of Salih, who slaughtered the she-camel, and the people of Jesus, who asked for the table spread from heaven and then rejected it. The commentators differ on who the "people" are: Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan name the followers of Jesus, as-Suddi the Quraysh who wanted al-Safa turned to gold, and Muqatil the Children of Israel who questioned their prophets and then disbelieved them.

Accounts of the occasion of revelation vary. Some report the question of Abdullah ibn Hudhafa about his father, others the question whether pilgrimage is due every year, and Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr link the verse to questions about the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham. Al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur stress that the prohibition targets questions whose answers would distress the questioner or impose hard obligations, while asking about what one genuinely needs remains permitted while revelation continues.

Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin emphasise that the blame falls on pedantic, contentious or idle questioning. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the pronoun in "sa'alaha" refers to the word "ashya'" rather than its meaning. Al-Qurtubi cites Malik, who disliked the multiplication of questions. The commentators agree that earlier nations were destroyed by the abundance of their questions and their disputes with their prophets.

This verse states that God did not ordain the practices the pre-Islamic Arabs invented around certain animals: the bahira, the sa'iba, the wasila and the ham. The commentators agree that the bahira is a she-camel whose ear is split and who is left free, neither ridden nor milked, yet they differ on what made her one. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrima say she is a camel that has borne five young, the last being male; Ibn Ishaq makes her the daughter of the sa'iba, while Abu 'Ubayda and al-Zajjaj describe a camel dedicated in gratitude.

The sa'iba is an animal released for a vow or for the idols, from which no benefit is taken. According to Ibn Ishaq, she is a camel that has borne ten consecutive females. The wasila, in most accounts, is a ewe that gives birth to seven young: if the seventh is male it is sacrificed to the idols, and if female it is spared; if a male and a female are born together, they say she has joined her brother and he is not slaughtered. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab gives another definition, that of a camel whose first two offspring are female. The ham is a stallion that has sired ten offspring, or whose offspring have themselves begotten; he is left free and is neither ridden nor burdened.

The commentators agree that these practices were the invention of the disbelievers and amount to lying against God. Al-Tabari adds that it was the leaders, such as 'Amr ibn Luhayy, who established them, while most of the followers did not understand that these were falsehoods. Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Kathir follow this reading, as does al-Razi, citing Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Ashur sees in the verse a warning against the innovations of the age of ignorance.

The verse thus sets revelation against the custom of the ancestors, and several exegetes draw from it lessons about blind imitation.

This verse describes polytheists who declared certain animals forbidden, such as the bahira, sa'iba, wasila and hami, and falsely attributed these prohibitions to God. When they were called to follow what God revealed and the Messenger, they replied that the ways of their fathers were enough for them. God answers with a rhetorical question of reproach: even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided? Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Ashur agree on the general meaning: the verse condemns blind imitation and the refusal to follow the Quran. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi add that one may follow only a knowledgeable, rightly guided scholar, whose guidance is recognised through evidence. Ibn Ashur holds that the verse concerns the dispute between the followers of revelation and those who invent lies against God, not the general question of independent reasoning and imitation in the secondary rules of law. On the forbidden animals, the reports vary in detail: Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi describe the bahira as a she-camel whose ear was split or whose milk was reserved for idols, the sa'iba as an animal dedicated to idols, the wasila as a sheep whose offspring were kept for certain uses, and the hami as a stallion released after a set number of mountings, while Mujahid, Ikrima and Abu 'Ubayda give different accounts. Ibn Kathir and al-Tha'alibi report, following a hadith of Abu Hurayra, that Amr ibn Luhayy was the first to introduce these practices.

In this verse God tells the believers to attend first to their own souls, keeping them from sin, and assures them that the straying of others will not harm them while they remain rightly guided. All will return to God, who will inform them of their deeds and repay them. The commentators agree on the core message: one must look to one's own uprightness, and the error of others does not burden the one who is upright. They differ on what 'being guided' means. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Kathir hold that this guidance includes enjoining good and forbidding evil, so that neglecting this when one is able is not true guidance; Abu Bakr narrated a hadith urging the changing of wrongs, and many took the verse as the strongest proof of this duty. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar, by contrast, said the verse applies to a time when counsel is no longer accepted, when each person answers only for himself. Al-Tabari, al-Razi and others report that the verse may refer to the People of the Book, to apostates, or may answer those who reproached Muslims for taking the poll tax from some unbelievers but not others. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi see it as a consolation for one who grieves over his people's straying. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi hold that counsel is obligatory as long as acceptance can be hoped for, while withdrawing into concern for oneself is appropriate when harm or discord is feared.

These verses address the bequest made at the approach of death and how it is to be witnessed. According to the majority of commentators, a believer who senses death nears should call two just men from among the Muslims to witness his will; if he is travelling and finds no Muslims, he may call two others from outside the Muslim community. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that if doubt arises about the witnesses, they are detained after the prayer, most identifying it as the afternoon prayer, while al-Hasan mentions the noon or afternoon prayer and Ibn 'Abbas and others the prayer of their own religion, and they must swear by God that they have neither concealed, altered nor betrayed anything.

Commentators differ on the precise sense of the word shahada here: al-Tabari takes it to mean the oath, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and others understand ordinary testimony that must be preserved and delivered, and many prefer this view. All agree that the verse warns against concealing or distorting testimony. If deceit is established, two heirs of the deceased take the place of the faulty witnesses and swear that their testimony is truer. The incident of Tamim al-Dari and 'Adi ibn Bada', concerning a silver cup, is the cause of revelation most often cited. On the testimony of non-Muslims, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, Ibn al-Musayyab and Ahmad held it valid during travel for bequests; Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa held it abrogated, while al-Zuhri, al-Hasan and 'Ikrima read "others than you" as "others than your tribe". The passage closes with a call to fear God and to obey.

The commentators explain these verses on bequests made during travel and how they are to be witnessed. When death approaches, believers should have their will attested by two just men from among themselves; if they are travelling and no Muslims are available, two witnesses from outside the community may serve. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that if the witnesses come under suspicion they are detained after prayer and swear by God that they have neither concealed nor betrayed anything nor sold their testimony for a price. Ibn Jarir and al-Baghawi say the prayer meant is the afternoon prayer, a time that all communities revere, while as-Suddi and Ibn Abbas in one report take it to be the prayer of their own religion.

Scholars differ on the meaning of "from among you" and "from other than you". Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Shurayh and others take them to mean Muslims and non-Muslims, and regard the verse as firm and not abrogated, the position also held by Ahmad ibn Hanbal. Az-Zuhri, al-Hasan and Ikrima understand kinship or tribe, while Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa hold that the testimony of non-Muslims is abrogated. Some regard the oath after prayer as an intensification of the oath.

If it later emerges that the witnesses betrayed or concealed something, two heirs of the deceased who are closest to him stand in their place and swear by God that their testimony is more truthful and that they have not exceeded the truth. The verses were revealed concerning Tamim al-Dari and Adi ibn Bada and a silver cup they had hidden, a case the Prophet ﷺ settled by having the heirs take the oath. The readings of "istahagga" and "al-awlayan" differ, and each reading has its justification among the exegetes.

These verses address the witnessing of a bequest when death approaches, especially while travelling when no Muslim is present. The apparent meaning is that two just witnesses from among the believers, or two others if you are travelling and no Muslim is available, should attend; after the prayer the witnesses are held and swear by God that they have neither concealed, altered nor taken any gain. If their betrayal becomes evident, two heirs of the deceased rise and swear that their testimony is more deserving. The commentators agree that these verses were revealed concerning the case of Tamim al-Dari and Adi ibn Bada' and the silver cup, on the obligation and legitimacy of witnessing, on justice as a condition where possible, and on swearing after the prayer. They differ on whether the testimony of non-Muslims is abrogated: Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab hold it remains valid for a bequest made on a journey, while Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa and the majority consider it abrogated; Ahmad ibn Hanbal regards the testimony of dhimmis as admissible. They also differ on the meaning of 'others than yourselves', understood by some as non-Muslims and by others as outside the clan, and on the prayer intended, which some take to be the afternoon prayer and others the prayer of the witnesses' own religion. The final verse explains that the purpose is for the testimony to be given truthfully and for the witnesses to fear the rejection of their oaths and disgrace, before calling to piety and obedience. Some scholars regarded these verses as among the most difficult in the Qur'an, both grammatically and legally.

This verse describes the Day when God gathers the messengers and asks them what their peoples answered them. They reply that they have no knowledge, for You are the one who knows the unseen. The commentators agree that the question serves to rebuke the peoples and establish the proof against them, since God already knows the answer. The meaning of the messengers' reply, however, is debated. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, followed in part by a report from Ibn Abbas, take it as a sign of courtesy towards God, the messengers leaving the matter to Him because their knowledge of outward things counts for little beside God's knowledge of hidden things. Al-Hasan, Mujahid and al-Suddi hold that the terror of that Day makes them forget the answer, which they recover afterwards in order to bear witness against their peoples. Ibn Juzayy and others see it as a politeness formula. Ibn Jurayj understands the question as concerning what the peoples did after the messengers died, a view al-Tabari finds weak since the question concerns the answer given in the messengers' lifetime. Al-Razi offers several explanations, including that judgment in the Hereafter rests on realities rather than conjecture, and that the messengers knew only outward things. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi record further opinions, but all these scholars agree that perfect knowledge belongs to God alone.

This verse recounts how, on the Day of Judgment, God reminds Jesus son of Mary of the favours bestowed upon him and upon his mother: He strengthened him with the Holy Spirit, enabled him to speak to people in the cradle and in maturity, taught him the Book, wisdom, the Torah and the Gospel, and had him shape clay into the form of a bird which, by his breath and by God's leave, became a living bird; he healed the blind-born and the leper and raised the dead by God's leave, and he restrained the Children of Israel from harming him when he brought them clear proofs, whereupon the disbelievers among them said: this is nothing but manifest magic. The commentators agree that all these wonders occurred by God's permission and not by Jesus' own power, which is why the phrase "by My permission" is repeated. They also agree that the passage is a reminder of grace addressed to Jesus, which at once rebukes the Jews who rejected him and the Christians who exalted him. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain "I strengthened you" as "I supported you" and identify the Holy Spirit with Gabriel. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi also offer the view that the Holy Spirit may refer to a pure soul or to the speech that gives life to religion. Regarding "kahl", some take it as the age between thirty and fifty, and draw from it the idea of Jesus' future descent. On the reading, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "sahir", referring to Jesus himself, while the majority read "sihr", referring to what he brought. Al-Razi notes that mention of the disbelievers in a context of blessings is explained by the envy that attends every favour, and thereby underlines its greatness. Questions of the unseen, such as the precise manner of resurrection, are not settled by the commentators and remain in the domain of mystery.

God reminds Jesus of another favour: He inspired the apostles, his sincere disciples, to believe in Him and in His messenger. They answered: 'We believe; bear witness that we are submitters.' Commentators differ on the meaning of 'inspiration' (wahy). Al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir and others take it as an inner inspiration or a casting into the heart, as al-Suddi and al-Hasan said. Abu 'Ubayda takes it as a command conveyed through the messengers. Others combine both: the command came through Jesus and the inspiration touched their hearts. Al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Atiyya read 'an' as explanatory. On who is addressed by 'bear witness', al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi allow either God or Jesus.

Al-Razi explains that the purpose of the passage is to rebuke the Christians: each of these favours shows that Jesus is a servant and not a god. The commentators agree that the apostles were sincere believers. They differ on the meaning of 'hawariyyun': al-Hasan says launderers, Mujahid fishermen, 'Ikrima chosen ones, and Qatada ministers. Al-Razi notes that faith is mentioned before submission because faith belongs to the heart and submission to outward conduct, an idea Ibn Sa'di also expresses when he joins outward Islam and inward faith.

The mention of the apostles leads into the story of the table sent down from heaven. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari report that they asked for this sign. Some commentators say the request came before they saw the signs, others that it came after their faith.

The commentators explain that the disciples asked Jesus whether his Lord could send down to them a table spread with food from heaven. The plain meaning is that they wanted him to ask God for this favour, and Jesus answered by telling them to fear God if they were believers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi agree that the disciples did not doubt God's power; they sought reassurance, or wished to know whether God would grant their request, since the verb 'to be able' can also mean 'to obey' or 'to answer'. Al-Zamakhshari, by contrast, took the wording literally and concluded that the disciples were not sincere believers; Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Razi and others rejected this and held that they were believers whose words were improper. The reading of al-Kisa'i, attributed to 'Ali, 'A'isha and Ibn 'Abbas, 'tastati'u rabbaka' (can you ask your Lord), is often presented as removing the difficulty.

There is broad agreement that 'ma'ida' is a table with food on it, though scholars differ on its etymology, deriving it either from giving or from moving. They also differ on what the table contained: Ibn 'Abbas mentions a fish and loaves, others mention food of every kind except meat, and al-Hasan and Mujahid held that the table was never sent down. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari favour the view that it was sent down, relying on God's words 'I will send it down to you' and on reports traced to 'Ammar ibn Yasir; these reports also include a warning against cheating and hoarding. Some of these narrations are regarded as weak, and commentators vary in how far they accept them.

Finally, Jesus's reply 'fear God' is read in several ways: as a warning against demanding miracles after faith, as a call not to doubt God's power, or as a reminder not to ask for what no earlier nation had asked for.

This verse recounts the disciples' request that Jesus ask God to send down a table from heaven. The commentators explain that their aims were to eat from it, to have their hearts set at rest, to know with certainty that Jesus spoke truly, and to bear witness to the sign before those who had not seen it. Ibn 'Abbas and others attribute the wish to pressing hunger, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi also report the view that they sought the blessing of the food itself. Al-Mawardi argues this because, had they been in need, they would not have been forbidden to ask. On the phrase "can your Lord...", Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Anbari hold that it did not express doubt about God's power but asked whether He would respond, whereas az-Zamakhshari reads it as a genuine sign of their doubt. The variant reading attributed to al-Kisa'i and 'Aisha, "can you ask your Lord", changes the sense to a request addressed to Jesus. Scholars also differ on "we shall know": some take it as a new knowledge gained through the sign, others as an increase of knowledge already held. Broadly, the commentators agree on the overall meaning and differ mainly on the interpretation of individual expressions.

The verse recounts Jesus, son of Mary, praying after his disciples asked for a table to be sent down from heaven. He asked God to send it so that its day would be a festival for the first and last of his people, a sign from God, and a provision, for God is the best of providers. The commentators agree that this prayer answered the disciples' request. The meaning of 'festival' (ʿīd) is explained variously: al-Suddi, Qatada and Sufyan take it as a day honoured and prayed on, Ibn ʿAbbas says that the first and last of the people would all eat from the table, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn ʿAtiyya understand a joy that returns, and al-Khalil a day of gathering. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi mention that the day of its descent was a Sunday, which is why Christians took it as a feast.

Scholars differ on whether the table actually descended. Mujahid and al-Hasan held that it did not, because the disciples, frightened by the warning of punishment for whoever disbelieves after its descent, withdrew their request. The majority, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi, held that it descended, since God said 'I will send it down to you' and His promise does not fail. Accounts of its content vary: bread and fish, a fish tasting of every food, fruits of Paradise, and the story of some who stole from it and were transformed into apes and swine. Ibn Kathir and other commentators regard many of these narrations as weak, and the Qur'anic text itself does not describe them.

God tells Jesus son of Mary that He will send down the table upon the disciples, and that whoever among them disbelieves after it will be punished with a punishment unlike any He has inflicted on anyone in the worlds. The commentators agree that the threat targets one who denies after witnessing the sign, since his guilt is greater. They differ on whether the table actually descended. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Razi and al-Qurtubi hold that it did, because God states it as a firm promise, and the warning attached to it does not cancel that promise. Al-Hasan and Mujahid hold that it never came down, because the disciples withdrew their request once they heard the condition; Mujahid even takes the table as a parable God gave to deter people from demanding signs. The accounts of the table's contents vary widely: Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' describe bread and fish, 'Ammar ibn Yasir describes bread and meat or fruit from Paradise, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr says it held everything except meat. Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan regard most of these reports as weak and keep only what is well attested. Several scholars, including al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi, say the punishment may be transformation into apes and swine in this life or a punishment in the next, and that 'the worlds' means the people of that time or all creation. Ibn 'Ashur focuses on the lesson about the disciples' faith and the reliability of God's promise, setting aside the details of the meal.

This verse recounts that Allah will ask Jesus, son of Mary, whether he told people to take him and his mother as two gods besides Allah. Jesus replies by glorifying God and disowning the claim, leaving knowledge to Allah. The commentators differ on when this exchange takes place. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj and most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi, hold that it will occur on the Day of Resurrection, to rebuke the Christians before all creation, citing the context and the following verse about the day when truthfulness benefits the truthful. Al-Sudi and al-Tabari hold that it took place when God raised Jesus up, al-Tabari relying on the word 'idh', which denotes the past, while Ibn Kathir judges that a conditional clause does not imply that the act occurred. All agree that the question is rhetorical, meant as a reproach, and that Jesus never said this. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and al-Baydawi explain that the Christians are addressed as worshippers of two gods, though they did not divinise Mary, since by deifying the son they were logically bound to treat his mother likewise. Al-Razi and al-Alusi note that 'dun' may signify difference or association. On the word 'nafs', Ibn 'Abbas and most scholars read it as the hidden or unseen, al-Zajjaj as the inner reality, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat it as a stylistic echo, and al-Alusi and al-Shawkani reject its application to God's essence without such an echo. Together these readings affirm Jesus' servanthood and the complete knowledge of God.

This verse records Jesus's answer when God questions him about the claim of his followers that he and his mother were two deities besides God. Jesus disclaims the claim and states that he said only what God commanded him: worship God, who is his Lord and theirs. The commentators differ on when this exchange takes place. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most exegetes, including Qatada and Ibn Abbas, place it on the Day of Resurrection before all creation, while al-Suddi, and one view reported by al-Tabari, place it at the moment God raised Jesus to heaven.

The word tawaffi is also read in different ways. Most commentators, among them al-Razi, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi, take it to mean Jesus being raised up to heaven. Al-Hasan notes that the term also means death and sleep. Al-Jubba'i understood it as an actual death, a view Ibn Kathir does not accept.

The exegetes agree that raqib means the watchful guardian of people's deeds, and that God is witness over all things. They differ on the request for forgiveness: some say it refers to forgiveness through repentance before death, while al-Razi and Ibn Juzayy read it as full submission of the matter to God's will. Al-Zamakhshari argues that the divine names al-'Aziz al-Hakim suit the context of submission better than al-Ghafur al-Rahim.

On the linguistic side, commentators debate whether the particle 'an in 'an u'budu Allah is explanatory or serves as an apposition, and al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan discuss these analyses at length.

This verse records God's words to Jesus on the Day of Resurrection and Jesus's reply, in which he disowns any claim to divinity for himself or his mother and leaves the fate of the people to God. The commentators give the plain sense: if God punishes those who died in disbelief, they are His servants and no one may question Him; if He forgives those who repented and believed, it is because He is the Mighty, whom nothing can resist, and the Wise, who acts only with wisdom. Most agree that the phrase hands the matter over to God rather than explicitly asking for forgiveness, which is why Jesus does not say 'the Forgiving, the Merciful'. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir place the scene on the Day of Judgment, though al-Tabari suggests it may have occurred when Jesus was raised, based on the past tense, while Ibn Kathir prefers the first view. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Tabari read the question as a rebuke aimed at the Christians. Al-Razi holds that forgiving associationism is possible in principle according to Sunni doctrine and the majority of Basran Mu'tazilites, and that the conditional form does not imply it will happen. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite the hadith of Abu Dharr, in which the Prophet ﷺ recited this verse through the night while praying for his community. Ibn al-Qayyim sees it as a model of courtesy toward God, since forgiveness flows from full power and full knowledge. Ibn 'Uthaymin specifies that the servanthood meant is the servanthood of creation. The variant reading 'the Forgiving, the Merciful' appears in some codices but is not the Qur'anic text, and commentators note that the attributes of might and wisdom keep the verse consistent with both of its conditions.

The commentators explain that God says this is the Day on which the truthfulness of the truthful will benefit them. For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they abide forever, with God pleased with them and they pleased with Him, and that is the great triumph. Al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Kathir and most others agree that this day is the Day of Resurrection and that the truthfulness meant is the truthfulness practised in this world, such as keeping covenants, believing in and confirming the messengers, and sincerity in deeds. Al-Mawardi notes that this truthfulness may concern covenants, the confirmation of the prophets, testimony to the prophets' delivery of the message, or the admission of one's own deeds. On the reading, Nafi' alone reads yawma with a fatha. Al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj take it as an adverbial of time. The Kufans allow its indeclinable form because of its construction with a verb, while the Basrans reject this, and al-Tabari prefers the nominative reading followed by most readers. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Zamakhshari hold that the words chiefly concern Jesus, while most exegetes take them as a general rule for every truthful person. Al-Razi says that the Garden, compared with God's good pleasure, is almost nothing, so he emphasises the latter. Ibn al-Qayyim notes that being pleased with God is a duty and a fruit of faith, while Ibn Sa'di and others understand the great triumph as deliverance from the Fire and entry into Paradise.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the account of the dialogue between God and Jesus, son of Mary, concerning the Christians. Its plain meaning is that dominion over the heavens, the earth and all that is in them belongs to God alone, so neither Jesus nor his mother can be a god, since they are among the things He owns. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya read it as a rebuke to the Christian claim, by which God exalts Himself above what is attributed to Him, and they add that His power extends to everything, so that He can destroy as He created. Abu al-Su'ud and Abu Hayyan note that the word 'ma' is used instead of 'man', which some take as a general rule and others as a sign of the inferiority of those called divine, or as a way of showing that all creatures are subjected to Him. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi link the verse to the main themes of the surah: fidelity to covenants, divine sovereignty and accountability. Ibn 'Atiyya also allows that it may be addressed to the Prophet and his community. All agree that royal authority belongs to God alone and that His power is absolute.
